The full-support manuscript proves that an admissible integrable minimizer
of the zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has Stieltjes support equal to every overlap
scale in [0,1). The proof turns a hypothetical support gap into a constant
interval for the order parameter. Variational contact at the ends of that
interval conflicts with a strict curvature inequality inside it. Along the
auxiliary diffusion, the spatial gradient of the value function is a bounded
martingale. Full support makes this martingale's second moment equal to time;
its terminal correlation with Brownian motion gives the ground-state value.
The manuscript's further argument gives a smooth Stieltjes density, strictly
positive on $(0,1)$, and no atom at zero. Sections 9.1–9.2 derive this stronger
ordinary conclusion separately from the selected formal support statement.

This record reconstructs those arguments and follows the finite Gaussian
approximation into the separate QAOA manuscript. The latter claims that
finite deterministic circuits approach the SK optimum when system size tends
to infinity before circuit depth increases. Its circuit construction needs
additional approximation, synthesis, seed-removal and transfer arguments.
The two formal statements concern full support and scalar value
consequences; neither states QAOA circuit convergence. Their verification
scope is described at the end. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main] and
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

For independent standard Gaussian couplings $J_{ij}$, put

$$
H_n(\sigma)=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j,\qquad
\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n,\qquad
P_*=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma).
$$

For overlap $R_{12}=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i^1\sigma_i^2$, the covariance is
$nR_{12}^2/2-1/2$. Thus the convention is $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, with
$\xi''=1$. A centered Gaussian of variance $1/2$, common to all
configurations, removes the final constant without changing the expected
maximum. Every normalization below uses this convention.

Let $\mathcal U$ consist of nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous
functions $\gamma:[0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ with
$\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty$. Their Stieltjes measures satisfy
$\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t)$, including
$\mu_\gamma(\{0\})=\gamma(0)$. They are locally finite, but need not be
probability measures or have finite total mass. Support is relative to [0,1).

Let $B$ be standard Brownian motion. The control value and Parisi
functional are

$$
\Phi_\gamma(t,x)=\sup_{|\alpha|\le1}\mathbb E\left[
 \left|x+B_1-B_t+\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds\right|
 -\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s^2\,ds\right],
$$
$$
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0)-\frac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$

Controls are progressively measurable for Brownian increments after $t$.
For a general admissible coefficient, the solution and its spatial derivatives
are locally absolutely continuous in time on compact strips; the time equation
holds almost everywhere. The control formula fixes the solution. The PDE is
$\Phi_t=-\tfrac12(\Phi_{xx}+\gamma\Phi_x^2)$, with
$\Phi(1,x)=|x|$. Auffinger and Chen's zero-temperature Parisi formula and
attainment identify $P_*$ with $\min_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$.
The support theorem itself assumes a minimizer and proves a property of it;
it does not separately supply one. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]
and [Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 1 and proof of Lemma 3][ac2017].

passages.text: ### 2.1 Structure of the argument The proof begins with regularity on strips bounded away from terminal time. It makes the diffusion $X$ and the gradient moment $q$ available, so a first variation can show where the minimizer is in contact. On a constant interval, the shape inequalities and the rational certificate give the strict curvature needed to contradict that contact. The zero-interval case uses a separate heat argument, and the possible terminal plateau needs its own exclusion. These steps lead to full support and the two moment equalities. In this manuscript route, the value argument then uses bounded-martingale convergence and the attained Parisi formula to express $P_*$ as a terminal Brownian correlation and an integral of expected curvature. Section 6 defines the terminal martingale variable and proves these equalities. The fixed-$T$ Gaussian approximation recovers this integral through Euler coupling, orthogonal normalization and mean-preserving rounding. The QAOA theorem additionally requires rooted energy identification, classical synthesis, removal of temporary seeds and transfer to fixed angles. The main route is §§3–5, then §§6–7, then §§8.1–8.6; §12 compares the two formal interfaces. The original analytic details are in [OpenAI (2026a), §§2–7][fs-main], and the circuit construction is in [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–6][q-intro]. The density theorem in §§9.1–9.2 is a further consequence of support and the PDE, not a premise of the scalar or circuit construction. The positive-temperature route in §11.1 independently supplies the same bounded classical input used for synthesis. The probability consequence in §11.2 requires a separate fixed-word second-moment theorem. These branches explain why the two selected formal statements are not a formal proof of the complete circuit theorem. These destinations separate premises of the support proof from its consequences. They locate the detailed arguments behind the short paper's support and density theorem. **The diffusion and moment identity.** For any admissible $\gamma$, the compact-strip estimates justify defining $X,q$ and computing $q'=\mathbb E a^2$; see [§2.4](#strip-estimates) and [§3.1](#gradient-moment). **Variational contact.** Minimality, admissible mass addition and compact mass removal give $G\ge0$, its vanishing on support and the contact slopes. The steps are in [§3.2](#feasible-variation), [§3.3](#measure-contact) and [§3.4](#contact-slopes). **Strict curvature.** Admissibility and a positive constant $c$ on an interval suffice; minimality is not needed. The shape comparisons, algebra and limiting argument are in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons), [§4.4](#curvature-algebra) and [§4.5](#plateau-limit). **Exclusion of gaps.** Combine contact with the appropriate positive, zero or terminal argument. The cases have separate destinations: [terminal](#terminal-gap), [bounded](#bounded-gaps) and [initial](#initial-gaps) gaps. **Positive density.** Full support comes first. Differentiated moments then give [smoothness in §9.1](#smooth-density-consequence), and a local comparison gives [strict positivity in §9.2](#positive-density). **Value and circuits.** Retain the same minimizer and diffusion through [the value identity in §6](#scalar-value-identities) and [the finite Gaussian construction in §7](#finite-gaussian-approximation). [The circuit argument in §8](#qaoa-construction) requires additional theorems. ### 2.2 The regularity available before the proof starts **Proposition 2.1 (compact-strip regularity).** For $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ and $0\le T<1$, the value has bounded, jointly continuous spatial derivatives of every positive finite order on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$. If admissible coefficients converge in $L^1$ and their smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz terminal values converge uniformly to $|x|$, these spatial derivatives converge uniformly on each such strip. The bounds depend on the derivative order, the fixed strip and a common coefficient mass bound. Time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere across coefficient jumps. On an open constant interval, the heat formula supplies the additional time smoothness used in §4. The terminal estimate is $$ |x|\le\Phi_\gamma(t,x) \le |x|+\sqrt{2(1-t)/\pi}+\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\,ds. $$ It controls approach to $|x|$ without differentiating that cusp. The strip estimates justify the interior calculations and finite meshes; the terminal bound and integrability justify the later endpoint limits. The two roles must remain separate. Their uses depend on the region and limit. On a fixed $[0,T]$ with $T<1$, bounded spatial derivatives and locally absolutely continuous time dependence justify the Itô identities and Euler coupling. Across a jump of $\gamma$, the spatial derivative moments remain continuous and the time equations hold almost everywhere; this is enough for contact slopes and the endpoint chord comparison. Inside a constant interval, classical time differentiation permits the strict-curvature calculation. As $T\uparrow1$, the controls change: the displayed value bound, integrable coefficient tails and martingale convergence justify first variation and terminal value. No differentiated estimate at the terminal cusp is used. These are [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1 and its diffusion consequences][fs-reg]; [§2.4](#strip-estimates) reconstructs their uniformity. The hypotheses also have distinct uses. Zero field supplies evenness, $u(0,0)=0$ and reflection in the shape argument. The convention $\xi''=1$ fixes the curvature coefficients. Monotonicity gives bounded coefficients before time one and nonnegative coefficient jumps; it also turns a support gap into a constant interval. Integrability controls terminal tails and Fubini interchanges, while local finiteness of the Stieltjes measure is enough for compact mass removal. Minimality first enters through the variational inequality in §3; the constant-interval curvature estimate itself applies to an admissible coefficient without assuming it is a minimiser. [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]; [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [OpenAI (2026a), §6][fs-var]. ### 2.3 Which prior results play which role The imported ground-state formula supplies two facts with different uses. Auffinger and Chen's Theorem 1 identifies the ground-state limit with an infimum over $\mathcal U$. To choose a coefficient attaining that infimum, one must also use their construction in the proof of Lemma 3. In the cited arXiv v2, the theorem is on p. 3, the compactness construction is on pp. 7–9, and the lower-bound proof is on pp. 11–12. Here is the part of that construction which supplies the witness. Let $\alpha_\beta$ be a positive-temperature Parisi distribution function. The source bounds $\beta\alpha_\beta(t)$ uniformly on each interval ending before one. Helly selection and a diagonal subsequence produce a nonnegative, nondecreasing right-continuous limit $\gamma_0$. In the SK normalization, the source's weighted integral bound also controls $\int_0^1\beta\alpha_\beta(t)\,dt$. For every nonnegative nondecreasing $h$, splitting at $1/2$ gives $\int_0^1 h(t)\,dt\le4\int_0^1t h(t)\,dt$: the first half is bounded by $h(1/2)/2$, and on the second half $t\ge1/2$. Fatou's lemma then gives $\gamma_0\in\mathcal U$. Mass can concentrate at time one during this limit, so compact convergence alone does not identify the limiting control problem. Write the limiting measure of the time coefficients as $$ \nu_0(dt)=\gamma_0(t)\,dt+m\delta_1(dt),\qquad m\geq0. $$ For an arbitrary admissible control, let $S$ denote its terminal state with coefficient $\gamma_0$. To see why the terminal choice is admissible, let the original control be $\alpha$ and put $S_s=B_s+\int_0^s\gamma_0(r)\alpha_r\,dr$. For a cutoff $\tau<1$ use $\alpha_s$ before $\tau$ and $g_k(S_s)$ afterwards, where $g_k$ is a continuous function bounded by one and converging pointwise to the sign with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=1$. This control uses only information available at time $s$. At fixed $\tau,k$, first take the temperature limit; then let $\tau\uparrow1$ and $k\to\infty$. The continuous terminal evaluation has thereby approached $\operatorname{sgn}(S)$ without anticipating a future state. The endpoint atom then contributes $$ |S+m\operatorname{sgn}(S)|-|S|=m $$ to the reward and $$ \tfrac12m\bigl(\operatorname{sgn}(S)^2+1\bigr)=m $$ to the combined control and Parisi penalties. These contributions cancel. Taking the supremum over the remaining controls proves $P_*\geq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)$. The upper bound proved earlier in that paper gives $P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$. Therefore $$ P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma) \leq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)\leq P_*. $$ Thus $\gamma_0$ attains the infimum. The cancellation is a step in the imported existence proof; it is not an additional assumption about the Stieltjes measure $d\gamma_0$. In particular, $\nu_0$ here is the limit of coefficient-times-Lebesgue measures, not the order parameter's Stieltjes measure. The two measures must not be identified. [Auffinger and Chen, arXiv:1606.05335v2, pp. 7–12][ac17]. The cited theorem is stated for the almost-sure normalized maximum. Its expected-value formulation used here follows from Gaussian concentration. For $L_n=n^{-1}\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma)$, the Lipschitz constant in the Gaussian couplings is $\sqrt{(n-1)/(2n^2)}$. Hence $L_n-\mathbb E L_n\to0$ in probability. Since the almost-sure limit is the deterministic Parisi value, the deterministic sequence $\mathbb E L_n$ has the same limit. The full-support theorem below remains conditional on a minimizer; neither of the selected formal interfaces constructs one. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, Introduction, ground-state formula and its footnote][fs-main]. Auffinger–Chen–Zeng's infinite support does not exclude an interior gap. Their terminal-plateau observation anticipates one endpoint obstruction; the argument below supplies the quantitative boundary-layer proof used here. The full-support manuscript develops a rational coercivity route and credits Chen's 2026 theorem for the same full-support conclusion and smooth absolute continuity. Chen's Proposition 4.2 has the conditional crossing form $q''(t)=0\Rightarrow q'''(t)>0$; the cited rational certificate gives $q'''(t)>0$ throughout a positive constant interval. These are different sufficient mechanisms, and this record makes no priority claim for full support. [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1 and Remark 7][acz]; [Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 4.2][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. The transformed density comparisons also have antecedents in Lopatto's positive-temperature analysis and Chen's zero-temperature analysis; the rational coercive identity is the different step in the full-support proof. Zhou's positive-temperature interval-support result applies near the critical temperature, whereas Lopatto's cited theorem covers the low-temperature zero-field phase. Neither transfers full Stieltjes support to zero temperature on its own: for the minimizers, $\beta\mu_\beta$ converges vaguely on $[0,1)$ to the zero-temperature Stieltjes measure, while the unscaled Parisi probability measures converge weakly on $[0,1]$ to $\delta_1$. These are different measures and topologies. Convergence without an interval-specific lower bound can lose support information. The direct zero-temperature gap proof below is therefore essential. [Chen (2026), Remarks 1.4–1.5][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. Two later editions sharpen the comparison without entering the pinned September proof. [Lopatto, arXiv:2607.11756v4, Proposition 5.1 and (5.8)–Corollary 5.6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11756v4), proves a conditional curvature crossing on a positive constant interval. Its integrating factor makes a transformed curvature derivative strictly increasing, so the associated contact derivative decreases and then increases; it does not assert an unconditional positive third derivative. [Lopatto, arXiv:2610.00127v1, Theorem 2.3 and §8](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00127v1), works at positive temperature and positive external field. Its comparison requires one-sided bounds on the coefficient before and after the chosen time, a moment inequality and a stationarity equality. The subsequent moment bootstrap yields smooth, strictly positive density on a nontrivial support interval; a singleton support is a separate case. Neither theorem removes the hypotheses of the zero-temperature argument below. Here is an explicit example of the information lost in such a limit. It concerns admissible measures, not Parisi minimizers. Put $g=\mathbf1_{[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1)}$ and $q_n=1-n^{-2}$, and for $n\ge2$ define $$ \mu_n(dt)=\frac{g(t)+n^{-1}}n\mathbf1_{[0,q_n]}(t)\,dt +\left(1-\frac1n\int_0^{q_n}(g(t)+n^{-1})\,dt\right)\delta_{q_n}(dt). $$ The continuous part has mass at most $(2/3+1/n)/n<1$, so these are probability measures with a positive endpoint atom. Their density is positive throughout $[0,q_n]$, giving $\operatorname{supp}\mu_n=[0,q_n]$. Their continuous mass tends to zero and $q_n\to1$, hence $\mu_n\Rightarrow\delta_1$ weakly on $[0,1]$. For a compactly supported continuous test function on $[0,1)$, the endpoint atom eventually lies outside its support. Consequently $n\mu_n\to g(t)\,dt$ vaguely there, although the limit vanishes on $(1/3,2/3)$. Even the cumulative coefficients converge in the topology used for the PDE: with $\gamma_n(t)=n\mu_n([0,t])$ and $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$, their difference is $t/n$ below $q_n$, and $\gamma_n=n$ on the terminal strip of length $n^{-2}$. Thus $$ \|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_{L^1(0,1)}\le\frac1{2n}+\frac1n\longrightarrow0. $$ Every $\gamma_n$ is admissible, but $d\gamma$ has an interior gap. Minimality and the gap argument supply information that these convergences alone do not. An atom added at time one is likewise invisible to the coefficient on $[0,1)$ and hence to its PDE and variational functional; the zero-temperature problem does not select an endpoint mass. Control and gradient-martingale methods have antecedents in [Auffinger–Chen](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-014-2254-z) and [Jagannath–Tobasco](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04398v4). A finite-temperature theorem with smooth terminal value $\log\cosh$ does not alone establish the result with terminal cusp $|x|$. The required compact-strip and terminal estimates are supplied in [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [Chen–Handschy–Lerman](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4) supplies earlier zero-temperature regularity, control and uniqueness results (Theorem 4 for uniqueness). This is distinct from the earlier finite-temperature uniqueness result of Auffinger and Chen. [Montanari](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10897v2) and [El Alaoui–Montanari–Sellke](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00904v1) inform normalised discretisation and optimisation. The particular shifted Gaussian coefficient identity used here is proved in [OpenAI (2026a), §7][fs-cons].

The curvature argument needs estimates uniform over the approximating
coefficients. Here is the route from the control formula to those estimates;
all bounds are taken on a fixed strip ending before time one.

For finite-step coefficients and a smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz
terminal function $\psi$, the evolution through a step of height $c$ is
$$
\Phi(t,x)=
\begin{cases}
c^{-1}\log P_{b-t}(e^{c\Phi(b,\cdot)})(x),&c>0,\\
P_{b-t}\Phi(b,\cdot)(x),&c=0,
\end{cases}
$$
where $P_h$ denotes convolution with a centred Gaussian of variance $h$.
The heat formula preserves evenness, convexity and the spatial Lipschitz
bound. Along a controlled path $dY_s=\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds+dB_s$, the drift
of the value minus the accumulated control cost is
$-\gamma(s)(\alpha_s-\Phi_x(s,Y_s))^2/2$. It is nonpositive, and is zero
for the feedback control. This proves the stated control formula for the
smooth step problem, including attainability by its feedback diffusion.

Using the same control in two such problems and then taking suprema gives
$$
\|\Phi_{\gamma,\psi}-\Phi_{\widetilde\gamma,\widetilde\psi}\|_\infty
\le \|\psi-\widetilde\psi\|_\infty
       +\frac32\|\gamma-\widetilde\gamma\|_{L^1(0,1)}.
$$
The drift part costs at most the coefficient difference in $L^1$, by the
terminal Lipschitz bound; the quadratic cost contributes another half of
that difference. The supremum norm is of the difference of the values,
which is bounded even though each value grows linearly in $x$.
With $\psi_M(x)=M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$,
$0\le\psi_M-|x|\le(\log2)/M$. Choose simultaneously $\gamma_m\to\gamma$ in $L^1$ and $M_m\to\infty$.
These are two distinct requirements: $M_m\ge\|\gamma_m\|_\infty$ alone
does not force terminal convergence. This compatible approximation
determines a unique uniform limiting value. Its terminal bound,
given in §2.2, also follows directly: choose the zero control for the lower
bound, and use $|\alpha|-\alpha^2/2\le1/2$ for the upper bound.

To obtain spatial derivatives, choose $T<b<1$. Monotonicity gives the
uniform coefficient estimate
$$
\gamma(t)\le\frac{\|\gamma\|_1}{1-b}\quad(0\le t\le b).
$$
An $L^1$-convergent family thus has a common coefficient bound $\Gamma$ on
this larger strip. For its smooth step approximants, put $U=\Phi_x$.
The differentiated mild equation is
$$
U(t)=P_{b-t}U(b)+\int_t^b\gamma(s)P_{s-t}[U(s)U_x(s)]\,ds.
$$
Since $\|U\|_\infty\le1$ and
$\|\partial_xP_hF\|_\infty\le Ch^{-1/2}\|F\|_\infty$,
$$
\|U_x(t)\|_\infty\le\frac C{\sqrt{b-t}}
 +C\Gamma\int_t^b\frac{\|U_x(s)\|_\infty}{\sqrt{s-t}}\,ds.
$$
Substituting this inequality once into its own integral uses
$\int_t^s((r-t)(s-r))^{-1/2}\,dr=\pi$. It reduces the estimate to an
ordinary backward Gronwall inequality with integrable forcing. This bounds
$U_x$ uniformly on $[0,T]$ without any terminal derivative bound. Repeating
on successively smaller strips bounds each higher spatial derivative: put
one derivative on the heat kernel and the rest on $UU_x$; only the term
$U\partial_x^mU$ contains the new highest derivative. The remaining products
have already been bounded.

Uniform convergence of the values then yields convergence of every
positive spatial derivative. For a bounded twice differentiable difference
$F$ with bounded second derivative, Taylor's formula gives
$$
\|F'\|_\infty\le \frac{2\|F\|_\infty}{h}
                         +\frac h2\|F''\|_\infty\qquad(h>0).
$$
First choose $h$ small using the common second-derivative bound, then make
$\|F\|_\infty$ small. Iterate on derivative differences. Passing to the
integral form of the differentiated PDE proves local absolute continuity
in time and its almost-everywhere equations. No classical time derivative
at a coefficient jump, and no derivative of $|x|$ at its cusp, is being
assumed.

Finally, couple all feedback diffusions with the same Brownian motion.
On $[0,T]$, let $L$ be a common spatial Lipschitz bound for their drifts.
The difference of the two integral equations gives, for example,
$$
\sup_{s\le T}|X_s^n-X_s|
\le e^{LT}\left(\|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_1
 +\|\gamma_n\|_1\|u_n-u\|_{\infty,[0,T]\times\mathbb R}\right)
 \longrightarrow0.
$$
This is a deterministic bound under the coupling. The derivative bounds
one order higher ensure uniform continuity when derivatives are evaluated
at these moving points. Every fixed polynomial in the bounded derivatives
therefore converges in expectation. This is precisely the convergence
needed for the integrated curvature expression in §4; none of the forward
density scores or their quotients need converge.
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.3][fs-reg].

### 2.5 Order of approximation

The same symbol for a small error must not conceal changing background
objects. The following account fixes those objects before the indicated
limit. A single admissible minimiser and its associated diffusion are
retained throughout the scalar construction.

**Compact-strip regularity.** Fix a derivative order $k\ge1$, a cutoff
$T<1$ and a common coefficient $L^1$ bound. Coefficients converge in $L^1$
within that bound; spatial derivatives converge uniformly on the strip.

**Shape inequalities on a plateau.** Fix the height $c>0$ and a closed
interior neighbourhood. Choose step coefficients equal to $c$ there and
smooth terminal values with $M_m\ge\|\gamma_m\|_\infty$ and
$M_m\to\infty$. The coefficient and terminal approximations may be
chosen as one compatible sequence.

**First variation.** Fix $\gamma$, a feasible $\eta\in L^1$ and initially
$\epsilon>0$. Remove the terminal cutoff before letting
$\epsilon\downarrow0$. The terminal remainder divided by $\epsilon$ is
bounded by an $L^1$ tail of $\eta$.

**Terminal value.** Keep the chosen minimiser and diffusion fixed. Bounded
martingale convergence and integrability of $\gamma$ justify
$t\uparrow1$; no terminal derivative bound is needed.

**Finite Gaussian coefficients.** Fix $\gamma,X$ and $T<1$. Refine $N$
using the fixed-strip bounds, then control the remaining value tail by $1-T$.

For the plateau transfer, tail estimates for a fixed approximant may depend
on that approximant. The passage to the limit uses the integrated
polynomial in the scaled second, third and fourth spatial derivatives of
the value function and the common strip bounds; it does not require
uniform bounds on the auxiliary density scores. Sections 3 and 4 explain
the variation and plateau-transfer arguments, and §7 gives a complete scalar error
budget. The further choices used to produce a circuit appear in §8.6.

passages.text: **Proposition 3.1 (variational contact).** For an admissible minimizer, the potential $G(s)=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt$ is nonnegative on $[0,1)$ and vanishes on $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$. At every $s\in S$, $q(s)=s$ and $q'(s)\le1$, with a right derivative at zero. The minimisation takes place over nonnegative Stieltjes measures with an integrable cumulative function. Their total mass is free. We first derive the variation of the functional, then use changes of measure which preserve this admissible class. The result will be contact on the *existing* support; the exclusion of gaps comes afterwards. ### 3.1 The moment function before minimisation Fix any $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, without yet assuming that it minimises $\mathcal P$. Compact-strip regularity and Itô's formula give $$ u(t,X_t)=\int_0^t a(s,X_s)\,dB_s,\qquad q(t):=\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2 =\int_0^t\mathbb E a(s,X_s)^2\,ds. $$ The initial term vanishes because zero field makes $\Phi$ even and $u(0,0)=0$. Thus $q(0)=0$, $0\le q(t)\le1$, and $$ q'(t)=\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2\qquad(0\le t<1), $$ with a right derivative at zero. The integrand is continuous on each compact time strip, so $q\in C^1[0,1)$. These facts hold for every admissible coefficient. They do not yet say that $q(t)=t$. The source proves them by smooth approximation on $[0,T]$, $T<1$; it never differentiates the terminal cusp $|x|$ at time one. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][fs-reg]. ### 3.2 The feasible right derivative Let $\eta\in L^1(0,1)$ and suppose that $\gamma+\varepsilon\eta\in\mathcal U$ for $0\le\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, where $\varepsilon_0>0$. This is a feasibility hypothesis: an arbitrary signed bump in $\gamma$ need not preserve monotonicity. Since $\mathcal U$ is convex, it is enough to check that the endpoint $\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ is admissible. The formula below is the zero-field, $\xi''=1$ specialization of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, arXiv:1609.04368v4, Proposition 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). Their chord $\gamma_\theta=(1-\theta)\gamma+\theta\gamma_1$ gives this direction by taking $\gamma_1=\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ and $\theta=\varepsilon/\varepsilon_0$. Their class $\mathcal U$ permits unnormalized cumulative measures with finite cumulative integral, so this change of parameter also covers the scaling direction $-\gamma$. We reconstruct the detailed PDE proof from OpenAI's Lemma 6.1. For $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, put $\beta=\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$, $\widetilde u=\Phi_{\beta,x}$ and $D=\Phi_\beta-\Phi_\gamma$. Subtracting the two PDEs gives $$ D_t=-\frac12D_{xx} -\frac12\beta(\widetilde u+u)D_x -\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\eta u^2. $$ The choice of diffusion $$ dY_t^\varepsilon =\frac12\beta(t)(\widetilde u+u)(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)\,dt+dB_t, \qquad Y_0^\varepsilon=0, $$ cancels the first-order spatial term when Itô's formula is applied to $D(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)$. Its drift has absolute value at most $\beta(t)$, which is integrable. On $[0,T]$ the resulting identity is $$ D(0,0)=\mathbb E D(T,Y_T^\varepsilon) +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_0^T \eta(t)\mathbb E[u(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)^2]\,dt. $$ At coefficient jumps the time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere. The source obtains this identity by approximating both coefficients by monotone step functions with the same smooth terminal datum, and then passing to the limit using the compact-strip estimates. The control representation, applied with the same control on each side, gives the time-local difference bound $$ \sup_x|D(T,x)|\le\frac{3\varepsilon}{2} \int_T^1|\eta(t)|\,dt. $$ Hence $T\uparrow1$, at fixed $\varepsilon$, removes the terminal term even after division by $\varepsilon$. We obtain the exact finite-change identity $$ \frac{\Phi_{\gamma+\varepsilon\eta}(0,0)-\Phi_\gamma(0,0)} {\varepsilon} =\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t) \mathbb E[u(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)^2]\,dt. $$ As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, the coefficients converge in $L^1$ and have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms. On each fixed strip, their gradients converge uniformly and have common spatial Lipschitz bounds. Coupling with the same Brownian motion and applying Gronwall's inequality therefore gives $Y^\varepsilon\to X$ uniformly on that strip. The integrand converges to $\eta(t)q(t)$ for each $t<1$, and its absolute value is at most $|\eta(t)|$. Dominated convergence, followed by subtraction of the linear Parisi penalty, now yields $$ D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta] :=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0} \frac{\mathcal P(\gamma+\varepsilon\eta)-\mathcal P(\gamma)} {\varepsilon} =\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt. $$ If $\gamma$ is a minimiser, this derivative is nonnegative for every feasible direction. It need not vanish: the minimisation has one-sided constraints. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1, equations (6.1)–(6.2)][fs-var]. ### 3.3 Which changes of measure are allowed? Write $\mu=\mu_\gamma$ and $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu$, with support relative to $[0,1)$. Tonelli's theorem gives the useful identity $$ \int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt =\int_{[0,1)}\!\int_s^1dt\,\mu(ds) =\int_{[0,1)}(1-s)\,\mu(ds)<\infty. $$ This is weighted finiteness, not a bound on $\mu([0,1))$. In particular, there is no normalisation constraint requiring mass added at one point to be removed elsewhere. Define the tail potential $$ G(s)=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\qquad(0\le s<1). $$ It is continuous, satisfies $|G(s)|\le1-s$, and has $G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$ on compact strips, with one-sided interpretations at zero. The following two competitors suffice. | Change to the Stieltjes measure | Direction in the cumulative function | Allowed parameter | Consequence at a minimiser | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Add $\varepsilon\delta_s$, $0\le s<1$ | $\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$ | $\varepsilon\ge0$ | $G(s)\ge0$ | | Remove $\varepsilon\nu$, where $\nu=\mu|_K$ and $K\subset[0,1)$ is compact | $\eta_K(t)=-\nu([0,t])$ | $0\le\varepsilon\le1$ | $\int_KG(s)\,\mu(ds)\le0$ | For atom addition, the new cumulative function is nonnegative, nondecreasing and right-continuous. Its integral increases by $\varepsilon(1-s)$, so it remains in $\mathcal U$. This includes $s=0$: an atom there adds a constant to $\gamma$ on all of $[0,1)$. The point $1$ is outside the measure's domain and is not an additional competitor. The derivative formula gives $D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]=G(s)/2$, proving $G\ge0$ everywhere below one. For removal, choose $T<1$ with $K\subset[0,T]$. Then $\nu(K)\le\gamma(T)<\infty$. The measure $\mu-\varepsilon\nu$ is nonnegative for $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, so its cumulative function is nonnegative, nondecreasing and right-continuous. It lies between zero and $\gamma$, hence is integrable; also $|\eta_K|\le\nu(K)$. Fubini is justified quantitatively by $$ \int_K\!\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu(ds) \le\int_K(1-s)\,\mu(ds)\le\nu(K)<\infty. $$ It follows that $$ 0\le D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta_K] =-\frac12\int_0^1\nu([0,t])(q(t)-t)\,dt =-\frac12\int_KG(s)\,\mu(ds). $$ Since $G\ge0$, its integral on every compact $K$ is zero. The compact intervals $[0,T]$ exhaust $[0,1)$, so $G=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. If a support point $s$ had $G(s)>0$, continuity would give a relative neighbourhood on which $G$ stays positive. After restricting to a compact interval containing that neighbourhood, the defining property of support would give it positive $\mu$-mass, contradicting the zero integral. Therefore $$ G(s)=0\qquad(s\in S). $$ This step applies to atoms, diffuse mass and singular continuous mass. Removing individual atoms alone would not establish it. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.2][fs-var]. ### 3.4 Contact values and endpoint slopes At $s\in S\cap(0,1)$, the function $G$ has an interior minimum of value zero. Thus $G'(s)=0$ and $G''(s)\ge0$, giving $$ q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1. $$ If $0\in S$, the argument needs the zero-field initial condition in addition to the one-sided minimum. We have $G(0)=0$ and $q(0)=0$, so $$ G(h)=G(0)+\int_0^h(t-q(t))\,dt =\frac12(1-q'(0))h^2+o(h^2). $$ Nonnegativity for $h>0$ implies $q'(0)\le1$. This works whether or not zero is an atom. The equality $q(0)=0$ comes from symmetry, rather than from differentiating a one-sided minimum. If $0\notin S$, no condition $G(0)=0$ has been obtained or used. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.2][fs-var]. We have now proved, without any no-gap assumption, $$ G\ge0\text{ on }[0,1),\qquad G=0\text{ on }S,\qquad q(s)=s\text{ and }q'(s)\le1\text{ for }s\in S. $$ These are precisely the contact data used in §5. They make no assertion that every zero of $G$ belongs to $S$, or that $q(t)=t$ at a point outside $S$. Terminal, interior and initial gaps remain to be excluded. ### 3.5 What the first-order criterion does, and does not, establish There is also a global alternative to compact mass removal. Atom addition still gives $G\ge0$. Now replace $\mu$ by $(1-\varepsilon)\mu$, or equivalently $\gamma$ by $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$, for $0\le\varepsilon\le1$. This preserves admissibility, and its direction $-\gamma$ lies in $L^1$, although it may be unbounded. The first variation in §3.2 therefore applies. The signed interchange is justified by $$ \int_{[0,1)}\!\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu(ds) =\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt \le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty. $$ Consequently $$ 0\le D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma] =-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu(ds). $$ Together with $G\ge0$, this gives $\int G\,d\mu=0$. Continuity then gives $G=0$ on relative support, including zero, as in §3.3. Finite weighted mass is sufficient throughout; no finite total mass or density of $\mu$ has been assumed. This ordinary argument uses the same integrable-direction first variation as the local removal proof. For the actual moment function associated with $\gamma$, the two potential conditions $G\ge0$ and $G=0$ on $S$ are also sufficient for minimality. This ordinary deduction explains exactly how much variational information has been extracted. For another admissible coefficient $\beta$, let $\nu=\mu_\beta$. The weighted identity above and $|G(s)|\le1-s$ make both measure integrals absolutely convergent, even when either measure has infinite total mass. Fubini gives $$ 2D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\beta-\gamma] =\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\nu(ds) -\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu(ds)\ge0. $$ Here the second integral is zero because $\mu$ is concentrated on its relative support. The control formula also shows that $\mathcal P$ is convex in its coefficient: for a fixed control, the terminal absolute value is convex in the coefficient and both penalties are linear; taking the supremum over the same control class preserves convexity. Therefore $$ \mathcal P(\beta)-\mathcal P(\gamma) \ge D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\beta-\gamma]\ge0. $$ This proves the converse. It agrees with the chord optimality criterion of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, arXiv:1609.04368v4, Proposition 4, printed p. 14](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). Chen's zero-temperature treatment obtains the same contact integral by testing $0$ and $2\gamma$ and then using weighted Fubini [Chen (2026), Proposition 3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12)][chen2026]. The compact-removal proof above keeps the local mass operation explicit. The converse concerns $G$ built from the PDE and diffusion of the same $\gamma$. It does not say that an arbitrary curve with these contact properties comes from a Parisi solution. Nor does it prove full support: the missing input is the strict curvature on an interval where the coefficient is constant, established next. The formal chord statement and the ordinary derivative bridge are distinguished in §12.1.

passages.text: The gap argument needs a property of the derivative $q'$, rather than convexity of the spatial function $\Phi$. We establish the following analytic input before using minimality. Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ be constant with value $c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, and let $X$ be its diffusion started at zero. Then $$ \begin{cases} q'''(t)\ge \dfrac1{1000c^2} \mathbb E\bigl[(c\Phi_{xx}(t,X_t))^4\bigr]>0,&c>0,\\[4pt] q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0,&c=0, \end{cases}\qquad t\in I. $$ Thus $q'$ is strictly convex for $c>0$ and strictly increasing for $c=0$. The coefficient may jump outside $I$ and may be unbounded near one, provided it is nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous and integrable. No support property or minimising assumption enters this statement. The positive-time restriction matters when a diffusion density is used; interval endpoints are handled later by continuity. [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][fs-curv]. The proof has two stages. In §§4.1–4.4 the coefficient is a positive monotone finite-step function with smooth terminal data. Shape comparisons and boundary estimates justify the [polynomial correction](#curvature-algebra) and its zero expectation. In [§4.5](#plateau-limit), approximants $\gamma_n,\Phi_n,X^n$ approach an arbitrary admissible coefficient. Only the integrated expression in spatial derivatives passes to the limit; the auxiliary forward scores need not converge. Bounds depend on a fixed compact strip and a common coefficient mass bound. The strictly positive right side is then justified for the limiting solution itself. ### 4.1 Why the uncorrected expression has no pointwise sign On a positive constant interval put $r=c\Phi_x$, $v=r_x$, $w=r_{xx}$ and $z=r_{xxx}$. In forward time, $r_t=-\tfrac12r_{xx}-rr_x$ and $dX_t=r(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t$. Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's formula gives $$ dr(t,X_t)=v(t,X_t)\,dB_t, $$ $$ dv(t,X_t)=-v(t,X_t)^2\,dt+w(t,X_t)\,dB_t, \qquad dw(t,X_t)=-3v(t,X_t)w(t,X_t)\,dt+z(t,X_t)\,dB_t. $$ Since $q'=c^{-2}\mathbb E v^2$, the drift of $v^2$ yields $c^2q''=\mathbb E(w^2-2v^3)$. The drifts of $w^2$ and $v^3$ are, respectively, $z^2-6vw^2$ and $3vw^2-3v^4$. Therefore $$ c^2q'''=\mathbb E\bigl[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4\bigr]. $$ These are interior-time identities. On a smaller constant interval the heat formula gives classical time smoothness and bounded spatial derivatives of sufficiently high order, so the local martingale terms have zero mean and the expectation differentiations are justified. Nothing here assigns a sign to $q''$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][fs-reg]. There is a concrete obstruction to reading the last display pointwise. For the smooth finite-step problem $c=M=1$ on $[0,1)$, with terminal value $\log(2\cosh x)$, the exact solution is $$ \Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+\frac{1-t}{2},\qquad r=\tanh x. $$ Indeed, $\Phi_{xx}+\Phi_x^2=1$. Writing $R=r^2$ gives $v=1-R$, $w=-2rv$ and $z=-2v^2+4Rv$. At $R=1/2$, $v=1/2$, $w^2=1/2$ and $z=1/2$, so $$ z^2-12vw^2+6v^4=-\frac{19}{8}<0. $$ This example lies in the smooth analytic class used below. Its diffusion density is $f_t(x)=e^{-t/2}\cosh(x)p_t(x)$, obtained from the heat transition formula, and integrates to one because $\mathbb E\cosh(B_t)=e^{t/2}$. It illustrates the necessity of the integration argument; it uses a smooth terminal value and makes no claim to be the zero-temperature minimiser. The displayed negative value is an exact elementary calculation. The heat formula itself is [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1][fs-reg]. The same pointwise obstruction occurs with the actual terminal datum $|x|$. For the admissible constant coefficient $\gamma_c\equiv c>0$, write $\tau=1-t>0$ and use the same heat formula: $$ \Phi_c(t,x)=c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}. $$ At $c=0$ its continuous extension is the heat value, whose derivatives are $$ a_0=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi\tau}}e^{-x^2/(2\tau)},\qquad b_0=-\frac{x}{\tau}a_0,\qquad d_0=\left(\frac{x^2}{\tau^2}-\frac1\tau\right)a_0. $$ At $x=\sqrt\tau$, $d_0=0$ and $b_0^2=a_0^2/\tau>0$. For fixed $t,x$, Gaussian convolution may be differentiated in $x$ through its kernel and expanded in $c$ near zero: exponential moments dominate every resulting polynomial factor. The apparent singularity of $c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}$ is removable, and its spatial derivatives through order four are smooth in $c$. Hence $$ d_c^2-12c a_cb_c^2+6c^2a_c^4 =-\frac{12a_0^3}{\tau}c+O(c^2)<0 $$ for all sufficiently small positive $c$, at that fixed point. This is an ordinary consequence of the constant-coefficient formula, not an arbitrary assignment of unrelated derivative values. It neither asserts minimality of $\gamma_c$ nor contradicts the positive expectation proved below; it shows why that expectation cannot be replaced by a pointwise inequality even in the absolute-value-terminal model. ### 4.2 The smooth finite-step problem and its boundary control Take $0=t_0<\cdots ### 4.3 Backward and forward comparisons, including jumps Use backward time $\tau$ on a single step. The equation is $r_\tau=\tfrac12r_{xx}+rr_x$. The logarithmic heat formula preserves strict positivity of $v$: its second spatial derivative is the tilted mean of the old second derivative plus the tilted variance of the old first derivative. Initially $v=cM\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)>0$, and positive rescaling at a backward jump preserves this property. Consequently $r(x)>0$ for $x>0$. Twice differentiating gives $w_\tau=\tfrac12w_{xx}+rw_x+3vw$. At the terminal endpoint $w=-2cM^2\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)\tanh(Mx)\le0$ for $x>0$. The boundary value at zero is zero, and the differentiated tails make the far boundary tend uniformly to zero. Comparison applied to $-w$ gives $w\le0$ on the positive half-line. Define $$ H=\frac{r_\tau}{r}=\frac{w}{2r}+v. $$ Oddness and $r_x(0)=v(0)>0$ make $w/r$, hence $H$, smooth and even at zero. Direct differentiation gives $$ H_\tau=\tfrac12H_{xx}+(v/r+r)H_x+vH, $$ $$ (H_x)_\tau=\tfrac12(H_x)_{xx}+(v/r+r)(H_x)_x +((v/r)_x+2v)H_x+wH. $$ The terminal signs are $H=(cM-M^2)\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)\le0$ and $H_x\ge0$ on $x>0$, using $M\ge c$. For the first comparison write $v/r+r=1/x+\eta(x)$, where $\eta$ is smooth and odd near zero. The radial extension $H(|y|)$ to $\mathbb R^3$ turns $\tfrac12H_{xx}+x^{-1}H_x$ into $\tfrac12\Delta H$. It is smooth at the origin, as is the extra drift, and $H$ tends uniformly to zero at infinity. Comparison on expanding balls proves $H\le0$. For the second comparison, $wH\ge0$ and $(v/r)_x=w/r-v^2/r^2<0$, so the zeroth-order coefficient has upper bound $2\sup v$. On $[\varepsilon,A]$, the two lateral errors are $H_x(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon)$ and $H_x(A)=o_A(1)$, uniformly on the closed step. Taking $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and $A\to\infty$ gives $H_x\ge0$. At a backward jump $r_{\rm new}=\alpha r_{\rm old}$ with $0<\alpha\le1$, $$ H_{\rm new}=H_{\rm old}-(1-\alpha)v_{\rm old},\qquad (H_x)_{\rm new}=(H_x)_{\rm old}-(1-\alpha)w_{\rm old}. $$ Thus both signs survive every jump. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.2][fs-signs]. For the forward score use $a_s=s_x$, temporarily distinguishing it from the Hessian $a=\Phi_{xx}$. The forward heat equation gives $$ s_t=\tfrac12s_{xx}-ss_x,\qquad (a_s)_t=\tfrac12(a_s)_{xx}-s(a_s)_x-a_s^2, $$ $$ (s_{xx})_t=\tfrac12(s_{xx})_{xx}-s(s_{xx})_x-3a_s s_{xx}. $$ The first step has $s=x/t$. Thereafter $a_s-1/t$ satisfies the linear equation with drift $-s$ and zeroth-order coefficient $-(a_s+1/t)$. For fixed smooth data this coefficient is bounded above on a closed step, independently of spatial truncation; this uses the tail bound and continuity, before asserting its sign. Comparison gives $a_s\ge1/t$. The last displayed equation then gives $s_{xx}\le0$ on $x>0$. At a forward jump, $$ s_+=s_-+\delta\Phi_x,\quad (a_s)_+=(a_s)_-+\delta\Phi_{xx},\quad (s_{xx})_+=(s_{xx})_-+\delta\Phi_{xxx}. $$ The backward signs and $\delta\ge0$ preserve the forward signs. A further comparison, not concavity alone, is needed. On $x>0$ set $d_s=s_x/s$, $d_r=r_x/r$ and $\rho=d_s-d_r$. The heat equation gives $s_t=\tfrac12s_{xx}-ss_x$, whereas $r_t=-rH$. Taking logarithmic derivatives yields $$ (d_s)_t=\tfrac12(d_s)_{xx}+d_s(d_s)_x-s_{xx},\qquad (d_r)_t=-H_x. $$ Since $\tfrac12(d_r)_{xx}+d_r(d_r)_x=\tfrac12(w/r)_x=H_x-w$, substitution of $d_s=d_r+\rho$ gives its equation $$ \rho_t=\tfrac12\rho_{xx}+d_s\rho_x+(d_r)_x\rho +2H_x-w-s_{xx}. $$ All three terms in the source are nonnegative by the comparisons already proved, and $(d_r)_x<0$. On the first step, concavity gives $r(x)=\int_0^xv(y)\,dy\ge xv(x)$, so $\rho=1/x-v/r\ge0$. Odd Taylor expansions give $d_s=1/x+O(x)$, $d_r=1/x+O(x)$ and $\rho=O(x)$ near zero; the tail estimates give $\rho\to0$ at infinity. Comparison on $[\varepsilon,A]$ therefore proves $\rho\ge0$ on each subsequent step provided its initial sign is preserved. Define $$ j=s\rho=s_x-(s/r)v. $$ At a forward jump, with $\alpha=c_+/c_-$ and $\lambda=(c_+-c_-)/c_-$, $r_+=\alpha r_-$, $v_+=\alpha v_-$, $s_+=s_-+\lambda r_-$ and $(s_x)_+=(s_x)_-+\lambda v_-$. Substitution cancels the added terms and gives $j_+=j_-$. Since $s_+>0$ on $x>0$, the sign of $\rho$ is preserved. The quotient $s/r$ extends smoothly and evenly across zero, with $j(0)=0$; reflection gives $j\ge0$ everywhere. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.3][fs-signs]. ### 4.4 How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful At a fixed positive time inside a step define $$ R=r^2,\quad K=rs,\quad b=-w/r,\quad B=b-2v, \quad L=-rs_{xx},\quad S_1=z+bv-2Rb. $$ The subscript on $S_1$ distinguishes it from the support set. The previous comparisons give $$ R,K,v,B,j,L,S_1\ge0,\qquad b=B+2v\ge0,\qquad Rb^2=w^2, $$ because $B=-2H$ and $S_1=2rH_x$. Here $s=-\partial_x\log g$ belongs to the forward heat factor, while $\partial_x\log f=r-s$ is the logarithmic derivative of the diffusion density. The signs have separate sources: $B\ge0$ comes from $H\le0$, $S_1\ge0$ from $H_x\ge0$ on the positive half-line, $j=s\rho\ge0$ from the relative-slope comparison, and $L=-rs_{xx}\ge0$ from forward concavity. Reflection extends these signs. The quotients were defined for $x>0$, where $r>0$ and $v>0$ by the tilted mean-and-variance argument in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons). At zero, $r$ and $w$ are odd, $r_x(0)=v(0)>0$, and division by $r$ is therefore division by a function with a simple zero. This gives the smooth even extension $b(0)=-z(0)/v(0)$; the other comparison identities give $j(0)=0$ and $S_1(0)=0$. Thus zero is not an omitted boundary of the integration. For $\mathcal D=r\partial_x$, direct differentiation gives $$ \mathcal D(R,K,v,b,j) =(2Rv,\ 2vK+Rj,\ -Rb,\ -z-bv,\ -jv+Kb-L). $$ Also $f_x/f=r-s$. Hence $\mathcal W(F)=\mathcal DF+(v+R-K)F$ satisfies $$ f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF). $$ This identity does not itself make the integral vanish. The tails give $r=O(1)$; exponential decay of $v,w,z,b$ and their derivatives; $s=x/t+O(1)$; $j=1/t+O((1+x)e^{-\kappa x})$; and $K=O(1+x)$. Every polynomial $F$ in $R,K,v,b,j$ and its differentiated expression therefore has at most polynomial growth. Meanwhile $f(t,x)\le C\exp(-x^2/(2t)+C|x|)$. Thus every term used below is absolutely integrable and $rfF\to0$ at both infinities. Smooth extension across zero prevents an interior boundary term. Integrating on $[-A,A]$ and taking $A\to\infty$ now gives $\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.4][fs-signs]. The proof has four separate checks: the comparisons supply these signs; the tail estimates make the correction integrate to zero; the rational identity below gives a positive remainder; and [§4.5](#plateau-limit) passes the resulting expectation inequality to the original coefficient. **Proposition 6.1 (terminal value).** For the minimizer and diffusion of
Theorem 5.1 there is a spin-valued terminal variable $U_1$ such that
$u(t,X_t)=\mathbb E[U_1\mid\mathcal F_t]$ and
$$
P_*=\mathbb E[U_1B_1]=\int_0^1\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt.
\tag{6.1}
$$
Its finite-cutoff tail lies in $[0,1-T]$. This proposition uses the
attained Parisi formula in addition to the support theorem.

The bounded martingale $u(t,X_t)$ converges almost surely and in $L^2$
to $U_1$. Its second moment tends to one because $q(t)=t$.
Since $|U_1|\le1$, $\mathbb E U_1^2=1$ forces $U_1^2=1$ almost surely.
Uniform integrability identifies $u(t,X_t)=\mathbb E[U_1\mid\mathcal F_t]$,
which is the conditional-expectation identity used below.

The drift bound $|\gamma u|\le\gamma\in L^1$ gives convergence of $X_t$
to $X_1$. Uniform terminal convergence of $\Phi$ to $|x|$, together
with convexity, gives $u(t,x_t)\to\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ when
$x_t\to x\ne0$. Thus $U_1X_1=|X_1|$, including when $X_1=0$;
no proof that this event has probability zero is needed.

Itô's formula gives
$$
\mathbb E\Phi(t,X_t)=\Phi(0,0)+\frac12\int_0^t\gamma(s)s\,ds.
$$
The terminal limit first gives
$\Phi(0,0)=\mathbb E|X_1|-\tfrac12\int_0^1s\gamma(s)ds$.
Subtracting the second half from the definition of the functional yields
$\mathcal P(\gamma)=\mathbb E|X_1|-\int_0^1s\gamma(s)\,ds$.
The ground-state Parisi formula identifies this with $P_*$.
The diffusion equation, conditional expectation and Fubini give
$$
\mathbb E[U_1X_1]=\mathbb E[U_1B_1]
 +\int_0^1\gamma(s)\mathbb E[u(s,X_s)^2]\,ds.
$$
Bounded $u,U_1$ and integrable $\gamma$ justify these terms.
Combining the identities and using stochastic integral covariance gives
$$
P_*=\mathbb E|X_1|-\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt
 =\mathbb E[U_1B_1]=\int_0^1\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt.
$$
The last integral is absolutely bounded by one because
$\mathbb E|a|\le(\mathbb E a^2)^{1/2}=1$.
Full support supplies $\mathbb E a^2=1$, whereas the value uses
$\int\mathbb E a$. Substituting the second moment into the value identity
would change the assertion. [OpenAI (2026a), §7][fs-cons].
The prediction error and the energy tail have different sizes:
$$
\|U_1-u(T,X_T)\|_2^2=1-T,
$$
$$
P_*-\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt
=\mathbb E[(U_1-u(T,X_T))(B_1-B_T)]\in[0,1-T].
$$
The first identity is orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal F_T$.
Martingale orthogonality removes the past Brownian component in the
second; Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the product by $1-T$, and convexity
makes it nonnegative. No uniform terminal curvature bound is needed.
The stochastic value calculation has a direct antecedent in
[Sellke, arXiv:2105.03506v4, Definition 1.3 and Lemma 3.11](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.03506v4).
There, “optimizable” means the contact identity $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$
on $[q,1)$, with $q$ the infimum of the support of the coefficient
function. Lemma 3.11 derives the finite-cutoff value identity by applying
Itô's formula to $\Phi$ and $xu$, before taking the terminal limit.
This is the same value-recovery mechanism used here, specialized to
zero field and $\xi''=1$.

A cutoff must retain the full Parisi penalty. Set
$\Psi(T,x)=\Phi(T,x)-xu(T,x)$ and
$I(T)=\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt$. Subtracting the complete penalty
from the finite-time Itô identity gives
$$
\mathcal P(\gamma)-I(T)
 =\mathbb E\Psi(T,X_T)
  +\frac12\int_0^T\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
  -\frac12\int_T^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$
Under contact the middle term vanishes. The final term is absent from
the displayed equality in [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke,
arXiv:2001.00904v1, §6.2, pp. 32–33][eams20]. Its sign is nonpositive,
so the upper bound by $\mathbb E\Psi(T,X_T)$ used there remains valid;
its magnitude tends to zero by integrability. This finite-cutoff
correction is consistent with the exact terminal identity above.

The reflection formula therefore gives, pathwise, $$ R_t=W_t+V_t-\min\left(0,\inf_{s\le t}(W_s+V_s)\right) \ge W_t-\min\left(0,\inf_{s\le t}W_s\right)=:R_t^0. $$ Indeed $0\le V_s\le V_t$ bounds the subtracted minimum by $\min(0,\inf_{s\le t}W_s)+V_t$. No independence of $V$ and $W$ is needed. Reflected Brownian motion $R_t^0$ has the one-time law $|B_t|$, so for $t>0$, $$ \Pr(|X_t|\le\delta) \le\Pr(|B_t|\le\delta) \le\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{\delta}{\sqrt t}. $$ Splitting at $|X_t|=\delta$, using spatial monotonicity outside and Cauchy–Schwarz with $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ inside, yields $$ 0\le m(t)\le a(t,\delta) +\sqrt{\Pr(|X_t|\le\delta)}. $$ First let $t\uparrow1$ and then $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves $m(1-)=0$. The compact-strip identity for $m$ now gives total mass one and the tail formula. Tonelli and (6.1) give the stated expression for $P_*$. In particular, $$ 0\le P_*-I(T)=\int_T^1(s-T)\gamma(s)\,ds \le(1-T)m(T)=o(1-T). $$ No numerical rate for $m(T)\to0$ or for the required spatial derivative bounds follows from this proof. The endpoint distinction also matters when comparing editions. [Sellke, arXiv:2105.03506v4, Lemma 2.9, equation (2.7)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.03506v4) states the expected-Hessian tail equality. In [version 6, Lemma 2.9, equation (2.8), and Remark 2.10](https://arxiv.org/html/2105.03506v6#S2.SS3), the general statement is an inequality; the remark obtains equality indirectly for even mixtures. The specialized zero-field proof above supplies its own endpoint argument from the shape and contact identities, rather than substituting $t=1$ into a compact-strip formula or relying on the older equality in its full stated generality.

passages.text: **Proposition 7.1 (finite Gaussian approximation).** For a fixed minimizer and its diffusion, the construction below has positive active normalizers for all sufficiently fine meshes at every fixed $0i$ vanishes on conditioning on the first $j-1$ coordinates; and the $j=i$ term is $\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{i-1},Y_{i-1})$. Also $\mathbb E[M_Ng_j]=\sqrt\Delta/c_j$ by orthonormality. Bessel's inequality applied separately to the orthonormal family $(g_j)$ and to the family $(Z_i)$ gives the vector estimates. Their union need not be orthogonal: $$ (A_j)_{j=1}^N=(\sqrt\Delta/c_j)_{j=1}^N+o_{\ell^2}(1), $$ $$ (B_i)_{i=1}^N= (\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{i-1},Y_{i-1}))_{i=1}^N+o_{\ell^2}(1). $$ Coordinatewise errors would not control a sum of growing length. Put $$ e_N=\|u(T,Y_N)-M_N\|_2,\quad \alpha_j=\sqrt\Delta/c_j,\quad \beta_j=\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1}) \quad(1\le j\le N). $$ The fixed-$T$ Euler argument gives $e_N\to0$. Bessel's inequality gives $\|A_{1:N}-\alpha\|_2,\|B_{1:N}-\beta\|_2\le e_N$. Also $\|B_{1:N}\|_2\le1$ and $\|\alpha\|_2\le C_T$ for sufficiently large $N$, with $C_T$ independent of the mesh. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$ \begin{aligned} \left|\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}(A_jB_{j+1}-\alpha_j\beta_{j+1})\right| &\le\|A-\alpha\|_2\|B_{2:N}\|_2 +\|\alpha_{1:N-1}\|_2\|B-\beta\|_2\\ &\le(1+C_T)e_N. \end{aligned} $$ The unindexed differences in this inequality use coordinates $1,\ldots,N$; restricting to the indicated subvector only decreases their norms. The rounding coordinate contributes at most $|A_NB_{N+1}|\le e_N+\sqrt\Delta/c_N$. Thus the dimension-free estimate is $$ \left|\sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1} -\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}\right| \le(2+C_T)e_N+\frac{\sqrt\Delta}{c_N}\longrightarrow0. $$ The index shift selects the Hessian at $t_j$; $Z_{N+1}$ serves rounding rather than another Euler increment. This estimate is a fixed-strip scalar correspondence, not a circuit energy identity. Hence $$ \sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1} =\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}+o(1) \longrightarrow\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ The same vector estimates also give an unshifted sum with this limit: $$ \left|\sum_{j=1}^N A_jB_j-\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\beta_j\right| \le(1+C_T)e_N\longrightarrow0, $$ $$ \sum_{j=1}^N A_jB_j =\Delta\sum_{j=1}^N \frac{\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1})}{c_j}+o(1) \longrightarrow\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ The latter is a left Riemann sum: $c_j\to1$ uniformly and the Euler coupling replaces $Y_{j-1}$ by $X_{t_{j-1}}$. Equal continuum limits therefore do not identify the finite expression needed by the circuit. The rooted energy calculation in §8.1 selects the adjacent pairing; the two finite pairings can differ, as [§10.4](#one-step-example) shows. Only afterward let $T\uparrow1$, obtaining $P_*$. The mesh count $N$ is unrelated to the spin-system size $n$. As in [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 7.2][fs-cons], these coefficients describe a finite Gaussian function, not yet a circuit on finite SK disorder. The QAOA scalar input also uses the tail estimate $0\le P_*-\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt\le1-T$, from nonnegative curvature and $\mathbb E a^2=1$. This estimate and the fixed-strip regularity facts must be retained beside the coefficient limit; they are not all clauses of the selected finite-Gaussian statement. They enter the construction in [OpenAI (2026b), §3][q-classical]. Thus, for every accuracy, the same chosen minimizer supplies a cutoff $T$ and then one finite function $F_N$ with $|S_{T,N}-P_*|$ below that accuracy. This is the finite scalar input. Turning it into spins for a finite SK matrix uses the separate AMP theorem in §9.4; turning it into a common QAOA word uses §§8.1–8.6. Neither operation is part of the Gaussian limit.

passages.text: ### 7.1 Error estimates at a fixed cutoff Fix the minimizer first and then $T<1$. The bounds below have constants depending on that minimizer and strip; they give an $N^{-1/2}$ rate there, not a rate uniform as $T\uparrow1$. Those derivative bounds are finite but have not been supplied as numerical inputs to an algorithm for choosing a mesh. The calculation is an ordinary deduction from the source's strip estimates, beyond the qualitative selected formal statement. Write $S_{T,N}=\sum_{j=0}^N A_jB_{j+1}$ and $f(t)=\mathbb E a(t,X_t)$, so $0\le f(t)\le1$. On the fixed strip let $K_T=\sup_{t\le T,x}|a(t,x)|$ and choose a spatial Lipschitz constant $L_T$ for $a$. Define $$ \delta_N=\max_{0\le j\le N}\|Y_j-X_{t_j}\|_2,\qquad d_N=\max_{1\le j\le N} \left|\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1})^2-1\right|. $$ These errors have a rate at each fixed strip, even if $\gamma$ has jumps. Put $\Gamma=\gamma(T)$ and $V=\gamma(T)-\gamma(0)$. Bounded spatial derivatives and the PDE give temporal Lipschitz constants $$ J=\tfrac12\|u_{xx}\|_\infty+\Gamma K_T,\qquad H=\tfrac12\|a_{xx}\|_\infty+\Gamma(K_T^2+L_T) $$ for $u$ and $a$, respectively, on this strip. No derivative of $\gamma$ is used. Brownian coupling gives $\|X_s-X_{\pi_N(s)}\|_2\le\sqrt\Delta+\Gamma\Delta$. Subtract the Euler and diffusion equations and split the drift difference on $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$ as $$ \gamma(s)\bigl(u(s,X_s)-u(t_j,Y_j)\bigr) +\bigl(\gamma(s)-\gamma(t_j)\bigr)u(t_j,Y_j). $$ Put $A_T=\int_0^T\gamma(s)\,ds\le1$ and $w_j=\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}\gamma(s)\,ds$. Taking a pathwise maximum over grid times, Minkowski and discrete Gronwall give, with $$ R_N=A_TK_T\sqrt\Delta+ [A_T(J+\Gamma K_T)+V]\Delta, $$ the bound $$ \delta_N\le\left\|\max_{j\le N}|Y_j-X_{t_j}|\right\|_2 \le e^{K_TA_T}R_N\le e^{K_T}R_N. $$ The recurrence weights the preceding maximal norm on interval $j$ by $K_Tw_j$; their sum is $K_TA_T$. The term $V\Delta$ is the monotone quadrature bound for the coefficient. For the martingale residual, Itô isometry and the same increment estimate give $$ e_N\le K_T\delta_N+ \sqrt T\{L_T\delta_N+L_T\sqrt\Delta+(H+\Gamma L_T)\Delta\}. $$ Thus $\delta_N,e_N=O_{\gamma,T}(\sqrt\Delta)$. These are deductions from the compact-strip bounds and stochastic identities, not quantitative clauses of the selected Lean statement. Since $a$ is bounded and Lipschitz, $d_N\le2K_TL_T\delta_N\to0$. Whenever $d_N\le1/2$, $$ \sqrt{2/3}\le c_j\le\sqrt2,\qquad |1/c_j-1|\le d_N,\qquad \|\alpha\|_2\le\sqrt{T(1+d_N)}. $$ These estimates give an explicit sufficient condition for all the required normalisers to be positive. They do not assume positivity for every coarse mesh. The first-moment identity in §6 makes $f=m$ nonincreasing, with $f(0)=1$. Its right Riemann sum therefore satisfies $$ 0\le I(T)-\Delta\sum_{j=1}^N f(t_j) \le\Delta\bigl(f(0)-f(T)\bigr). $$ Removing the last term adds $\Delta f(T)$, so $0\le I(T)-\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}f(t_j)\le\Delta$. The difference between the shifted interior sum and the integral is bounded by $$ \left|\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1} \frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}-\int_0^T f(t)\,dt\right| \le TK_Td_N+TL_T\delta_N+\Delta. $$ The first two terms replace the normalisers and Euler positions; the last is the preceding monotone quadrature estimate. Combining this with the vector and rounding-endpoint estimate gives $$ \begin{aligned} |S_{T,N}-P_*| \le{}&(1-T)m(T) +\bigl(2+\sqrt{T(1+d_N)}\bigr)e_N +\sqrt{\Delta(1+d_N)}\\ &+TK_Td_N+TL_T\delta_N+\Delta . \end{aligned} $$ In particular, for each fixed minimizer and $T<1$ there are finite $C_{\gamma,T}$ and $N_0(\gamma,T)$ such that $$ |S_{T,N}-P_*|\le(1-T)m(T)+C_{\gamma,T}\sqrt{T/N} \qquad(N\ge N_0(\gamma,T)). $$ The constants are not uniform as $T\uparrow1$. The [coefficient budget](#coefficient-budget) bounds $\int\gamma$ and $\gamma$ on each fixed strip, but numerical bounds for all strip derivative constants and an effective mesh threshold are not supplied. The scalar tail bound $(1-T)m(T)\le1-T$ uses only monotonicity of the first moment; Proposition 6.2 further makes it $o(1-T)$. All terms after this scalar tail tend to zero at each fixed $T<1$. Given a scalar tolerance $\zeta>0$, first choose $T$ with $1-T<\zeta/2$, then choose $N_0(\gamma,T,\zeta)$ so that their sum is below $\zeta/2$ for every $N\ge N_0$. This is the required finite choice of a Gaussian spin. The formula exposes the errors; it does not supply numerical values of $K_T,L_T,\delta_N,e_N$ or an effective mesh threshold. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1][fs-reg]; [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 7.2][fs-cons]. A diagonal can be chosen using these thresholds. For prescribed $T_m\uparrow1$, choose increasing $N_m$ large enough to make the mesh-dependent part of the fixed-$T_m$ bound less than $1/m$. An arbitrary increasing mesh schedule does not follow from the iterated limit alone. For example, the scalar array $$ h(T,N)=\min\{1,[N(1-T)]^{-1}\} $$ tends to zero in $N$ at every fixed $T<1$, but $h(1-1/N,N)=1$ for every $N\ge2$. This is an illustration of the quantifier issue, not an asserted error law for the SK construction.

On a single spin, let $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; $Z_i$ and $X_i$ act on spin $i$
and as the identity on the other spins. Also set
$Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
Then $X|\pm\rangle=\pm|\pm\rangle$ and $Z|+\rangle=|-\rangle$. The cost and mixer are
$$
C_{n,J}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_iZ_j,\qquad B_n=\sum_iX_i.
$$
The two evolutions act differently:
$$
e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}|\sigma\rangle
 =e^{-i\theta H_n(\sigma)}|\sigma\rangle,
\qquad
e^{-i\beta B_n}=\prod_{i=1}^n(\cos\beta\,I-i\sin\beta\,X_i).
$$
The cost evolution changes phases while preserving spin-basis probabilities;
the mixer combines amplitudes of different spin configurations. Cost evolution
alone leaves the initial uniform probabilities unchanged, and a mixer applied
first only multiplies $|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$ by $e^{-in\beta}$.
Alternating them lets the cost-dependent phases change subsequent measurement
probabilities. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022), §2,
equations (1)–(6)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).

A depth-$p$ state, with $p$ counting cost–mixer pairs, is
$$
|\psi_{n,p,J}(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)\rangle
=e^{-i\beta_pB_n}e^{-i\gamma_pC_{n,J}}\cdots
 e^{-i\beta_1B_n}e^{-i\gamma_1C_{n,J}}|+\rangle^{\otimes n}.
$$
Here the real angle vectors $\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta$ are
deterministic; $\boldsymbol\gamma$ is separate from the Parisi coefficient
$\gamma(t)$. A *word* means a finite ordered product of cost and mixer
exponentials. Its pattern and angles are fixed independently of $n,J$;
its cost operator depends on $n,J$. Define
$$
v_p(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
 \langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle,
\qquad Q_p=\sup_{\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p}v_p.
$$
The fixed-depth, fixed-angle infinite-size limit is the input from
Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou; it does not contain the later depth
conclusion; see [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).
The source target is $\lim_{p\to\infty}Q_p=P_*$. Its needed lower
bound has the literal quantifiers
$$
\forall\varepsilon>0\quad\exists p\in\mathbb N,
\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p:
\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
\langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle
\ge P_*-\varepsilon.
$$
The same finite list of gates and angles is used for every $n,J$; this is
a limiting expected-energy conclusion. A cost expectation is bounded above by its
maximum eigenvalue, and zero-angle padding makes $Q_p$ nondecreasing.
It therefore suffices to construct one finite word for every accuracy.
Fixed-instance convergence at increasing depth is a different quantifier
order. Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann's original QAOA argument obtains that
convergence by adiabatic evolution and its Trotter approximation, with depth
allowed to depend on the instance; it does not supply the size-independent
word required here. [Farhi–Goldstone–Gutmann (2014), equation (10) and
§VI, pp. 10–11](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1);
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

The construction first describes local operations on a large tree, where
neighbouring subtrees supply Gaussian inputs. Temporary random labels let
those operations implement the finite classical function of §7. The hard
steps are to implement its aggregations using cost and mixer gates, and
then to replace every use of the labels by ordinary gates while preserving
the energy. Only the resulting ordinary word is transferred to SK.

The choices are nested: fix $\varepsilon$, choose $T<1$, choose a finite
mesh, fix the bounded classical formula and helper probabilities, then
choose the finite gate approximations and remove the seeds. The constants
in a replacement may depend on the surrounding word and on those positive
helper probabilities. [§8.6](#qaoa-assembly-detail) collects the error
allocation before the final $n\to\infty$ limit.
The principal circuit inputs can be read as four local lemmas. Their
proofs remain in the cited manuscript; §§8.2–8.5 reconstruct the
mechanisms and show where each hypothesis enters.

**Smooth replacement.** Fix the height, a finite expression and channel
list, and the required derivatives. Uniform recursive weighted bounds,
convergence of operators and adjoints, and strongly commuting signals with
the stated joint exponential bounds permit substitution inside a fixed
surrounding sequence in the exclusion-gate class defined in §8.2. Constants depend on that fixed family. This is the input
used in §8.3 to replace classical aggregates by finite gates; see
[the foundations, smooth topology and gate calculus][q-gate-calculus].

**Helper contraction and synthesis.** Fix a bounded, finite, type-excluded
odd formula, zero on helpers, and positive helper masses. The contraction
converges smoothly at every cut and for the specified responses. For each
$\eta>0$, finite seeded synthesis gives
$$
\mathcal E(v)\ge\mathcal E(m)-2\eta-2\sqrt{p_H}.
$$
Section 8.4 receives this one fixed seeded word. The source inputs are the
[synthesis statements][q-synthesis-statement] and
[helper theorem][q-helper-statement].

**Seed removal.** Fix that finite seeded word and an energy tolerance.
Reuse the same Gaussian at every occurrence on a vertex. Packet control and
the one-particle comparison then produce one finite ordinary word with the
required energy error. The [seed-removal theorem][q-seed-statement] supplies
an energy conclusion, not merely convergence of seed marginals. It makes the
ordinary-word transfer in §8.5 applicable.

**Fixed-word transfer.** Fix one ordinary word and all its angles before
either size or degree varies. Its positive tree scaled-edge limit equals
its SK expected-energy limit, with the convention conversion in §8.5.
This [fixed-word transfer][q-transfer] closes the thermodynamic-first
theorem in §8.6.

passages.text: ### 8.1 Rooted realisation and the observable it preserves The fixed-depth spin–boson representation has an antecedent in [Boulebnane et al., Theorem 2 (informal), equations (10)–(11), p. 3][spin-boson]: as the degree grows with depth fixed, the symmetric tree state converges to a spin coupled to finitely many bosonic modes. The manuscript credits that representation, then proves the occupation, insertion and surrounding-circuit estimates needed below. Its additional task is to control the energy observable and substitutions inside a circuit, beyond identifying a limiting state. [OpenAI (2026b), §2][q-fock]. The immediate task is to realise the finite Gaussian spin from §7 in a space where its shifted correlation sum becomes an energy observable. We will identify that sum with a rooted quadratic form, then relate the same form to the scaled edge energy of a fixed circuit; §8.5 supplies the final transfer to SK. For an ordinary depth-$p$ word, this tree calculation uses only finitely many spins. Conjugate $Z_iZ_j$ backwards through the circuit. A mixer rotates the spins already in its support without enlarging that support. In a cost layer all edge factors commute, so factors disjoint from the current support commute past the other factors and cancel. The remaining factors enlarge support by at most one graph step. After $p$ pairs, the edge expectation therefore depends only on its radius-$p$ backward light cone. On the $(D+1)$-regular tree this contains at most $2\sum_{r=0}^pD^r$ vertices; the spins outside factor out of the product-state expectation. Thus fixed depth gives fixed tree height, although the number of children grows with $D$. This locality explains the finite tree calculation; the equality with dense SK is the separate transfer theorem in §8.5. [Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann (2014), §II, equations (14)–(26)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1). On a rooted tree, factor a circuit as $U=(\bigotimes_jU_j)u$, where each $U_j$ contains operations wholly in child subtree $j$. Conjugating a root observable $P$ reduces to $u^*Pu$; its insertion vector is $u^*Pu\,\mathrm{vac}$, centered when its vacuum mean is zero. This factorization is why child operations enter the recursion below. The first change of setting preserves a specified quadratic form. At height zero the pointed space is $\mathsf k=\mathbb C^2\otimes L^2(\text{seed})$, with distinguished vector $\omega=|+\rangle\otimes1$. Recursively, $$ \mathcal H_0=\mathsf k,\qquad \mathcal H_{h+1}=\mathsf k\otimes\Gamma_s(\mathcal H_h^\circ), $$ where $\mathcal H_h^\circ$ is the orthogonal complement of the vacuum and $\Gamma_s$ is symmetric Fock space. A particle here is one child subtree whose state differs from its vacuum. It is not one physical spin. The occupation embedding identifies a symmetric state with $m$ nonvacuum children among $D$ available children with its $m$-particle vector, using the factor $\binom Dm^{-1/2}$. Adding empty descendants gives compatible embeddings between heights. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, pointed spaces and occupation embeddings][q-fock]. For a child direction $f$, write $q(f)=a^*(f)+a(f)$ and $W(f)=e^{iq(f)}$. Explicitly, $\Gamma_s(H)=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}H^{\otimes_s m}$, with vacuum $\Omega$ in sector zero. On sector $m$, $a^*(f)\psi=\sqrt{m+1}\operatorname{Sym}(f\otimes\psi)$, and $a(f)$ is its adjoint. The number operator is multiplication by $m$; more generally $d\Gamma(A)$ sums $A$ over those $m$ child factors. The vacuum characteristic function $\langle\Omega,e^{itq(f)}\Omega\rangle=e^{-t^2\|f\|^2/2}$ fixes the Gaussian normalization. In the real classical sector, a centred child vector $f$ produces a parent Gaussian position $\mathsf G(f)=q(f)$ with $$ \mathbb E[\mathsf G(f)\mathsf G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle, \qquad \|[\mathsf G(f)-\mathsf G(g)]\mathrm{vac}\|=\|f-g\|. $$ The receiving root's own seed is a separate, independent tensor factor. The root shift $$ \mathsf Lf=\omega\otimes a^*(f)\Omega $$ is an isometry on centred vectors, and is extended by zero on the vacuum. Its adjoint extracts the root-vacuum, one-child component, including a constant receiving-root seed. For a classical function of orthonormal Gaussian positions, this is its first Gaussian chaos. These covariance, independence and projection properties have distinct roles in the next calculation. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, root shift and classical first chaos][q-root-energy] [OpenAI (2026b), §2, classical Gaussian positions][q-gaussian]. Start with the standard root seed $g_0=S$ and recursively set $Z_{j+1}=\mathsf G(g_j)$. Suppose $g_0,\ldots,g_{j-1}$ are centred orthonormal vectors. The covariance identity gives independent standard normals $Z_1,\ldots,Z_j$. In the scalar construction of §7, the multiplier of $Z_j$ in $g_j$ depends only on its predecessors. Conditional centring therefore makes $g_j$ orthogonal to $g_1,\ldots,g_{j-1}$, and the chosen normaliser $c_j$ gives unit norm. Independence of the receiving-root seed gives orthogonality to $g_0$. This closes the induction. Compatible height embeddings ensure that the earlier variables are the same variables when the formula is embedded at greater height. Oddness of $u$ and evenness of $a$ make $Y_j$ and $g_j$ odd under simultaneous seed reversal. The extra centred rounding variable $2F_{\rm G}(Z_{N+1})-1$ is odd as well, so $F_N$ is centred. It is independent of the receiving-root seed, hence $\langle F_N,g_0\rangle=0=A_0$. With $A_j,B_{j+1}$ as in §7, first-chaos projection gives $$ \mathsf L^*F_N=\sum_{j=0}^NB_{j+1}g_j,\qquad \mathcal E(F_N):=\operatorname{Re}\langle F_N,\mathsf LF_N\rangle =\sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1}. $$ Thus the construction identifies both the scalar law and the required rooted energy. The Gaussian covariance rule does not declare distinct calculations on shared descendant subtrees independent. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, “A finite Gaussian formula and its rooted energy”][q-rooted-classical]. The connection to an edge observable is another statement. Let $f_D$ be centred, invariant under rooted permutations of complete child subtrees, and supported at a fixed finite radius. Suppose its occupation embedding converges strongly to $v$, with a uniformly bounded expected top-generation occupation $\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$. Put $M=D+1$ and $R_M=\sqrt{1-\mathsf N/M}$. To see the decomposition, delete the distinguished edge and project onto the vacuum on either resulting half-tree. There are four pairings. The vacuum–vacuum pairing is zero by centring. If only one side is excited, the other side forces the root and all remaining branches into their vacuum; root symmetry gives the term $M^{-1/2}\langle\mathsf L^*f_D,R_Mf_D\rangle$ or its conjugate. In the pairing where both sides are excited, each projected vector has squared norm $M^{-1}\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$ by symmetry among the $M$ branches. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds their pairing by that same quantity. Finally, deleting one vacuum child multiplies the $m$-particle sector by $\sqrt{\binom{M-1}{m}/\binom{M}{m}}=\sqrt{1-m/M}$, which identifies $R_M$. Thus the exact edge decomposition is $$ \langle f_{D,i},f_{D,j}\rangle =\frac2{\sqrt M}\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathsf L^*f_D,R_Mf_D\rangle +\varepsilon_D, \qquad |\varepsilon_D|\le\frac{\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle}{M}. $$ Vacuum deletion also gives $\|R_Mf_D-f_D\|^2\le M^{-1}\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$. Consequently, $$ \lim_{D\to\infty}\frac{\sqrt D}{2} \langle f_{D,i},f_{D,j}\rangle=\mathcal E(v). $$ Strong convergence alone does not control the scaled remainder. The occupation estimate is supplied later for the relevant finite circuits. The occupation assumption cannot be dropped merely because vectors converge in norm. For orthogonal unit vectors $e_m$ in sector $m$, $\psi_k=\sqrt{1-1/k}\,\Omega+k^{-1/2}e_{k^2}$ tends to $\Omega$ in norm, whereas $\langle\psi_k,\mathsf N\psi_k\rangle=k$. The elementary continuity bound $$ |\mathcal E(v)-\mathcal E(w)| \le(\|v\|+\|w\|)\|v-w\| $$ will control every subsequent approximation after the observable has been identified. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Energy as a root shift,” including its exact finite-degree decomposition][q-root-energy]. The three identifications use different information: First, passing from the finite Gaussian formula to the rooted classical sector preserves the joint Gaussian law and the same $F_N$. passages.text: #### 8.1.1 One depth, three descriptions of the energy A single cost–mixer pair tests the signs and normalizations in this change of objects. Use the positive cost $C_{n,J}$ of §8 and $U=e^{-i\beta B_n}e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}$; the symbol $\theta$ here is a cost angle, not the Parisi coefficient. Put $c=\cos(2\beta)$ and $s=\sin(2\beta)$. The Pauli identities are $$ e^{i\beta X}Ze^{-i\beta X}=cZ+sY,\qquad e^{i\alpha Z_iZ_j}Y_je^{-i\alpha Z_iZ_j} =Y_j\cos(2\alpha)+Z_iX_j\sin(2\alpha). $$ The mixed term $Z_iY_j$ therefore has cost-state expectation $$ \sin(2\theta J_{ij}/\sqrt n) \prod_{k\ne i,j}\cos(2\theta J_{jk}/\sqrt n). $$ The other mixed term exchanges $i$ and $j$. The $Z_iZ_j$ term has zero expectation. The $Y_iY_j$ term can be nonzero on an individual complete graph, but its expectation after the cost gate is independent of $J_{ij}$: $Y_iY_j$ commutes with that edge cost. Multiplying by $J_{ij}$ and averaging therefore removes it, even in the presence of triangles. For a standard Gaussian $J$, $$ \mathbb E\cos(aJ)=e^{-a^2/2},\qquad \mathbb E[J\sin(aJ)]=ae^{-a^2/2}. $$ Averaging the mixed terms and summing the $n(n-1)/2$ unordered edges gives $$ \frac1n\mathbb E_J\langle C_{n,J}\rangle =\frac{n-1}{n}\,\theta\sin(4\beta) e^{-2\theta^2(n-1)/n}. $$ This agrees with [Farhi et al., equation (62)][fggz]. With energy maximization, $\theta=1/2$, $\beta=\pi/8$ gives the limiting value $1/(2\sqrt e)$; their minimization example uses $\beta=-\pi/8$ and the negative value. For the positive cost $D^{-1/2}\sum_{\{i,j\}}Z_iZ_j$ on the $(D+1)$-regular tree, each endpoint has $D$ other neighbours. The same calculation now has no common-neighbour contribution and yields $$ \langle Z_oZ_v\rangle =\sin(4\beta)\sin(2\theta/\sqrt D) \cos^D(2\theta/\sqrt D). $$ Multiplying by $\sqrt D/2$ and letting $D\to\infty$ gives $\theta e^{-2\theta^2}\sin(4\beta)$, the same limit as finite SK. This checks the factor $1/2$ and the degree convention in §8.5. Finally let $e=Z\mathrm{vac}=|-\rangle\otimes\Omega$ and $Q=q(e)$ in the rooted description. Its vacuum law is standard normal. The depth-one root operation is $u=e^{-i\beta X}e^{-i\theta ZQ}$. Using $Y|+\rangle=-i|-\rangle$, its insertion is $$ v=u^*Zu\,\mathrm{vac} =|-\rangle\otimes[c-is\cos(2\theta Q)]\Omega +|+\rangle\otimes s\sin(2\theta Q)\Omega. $$ The root shift retains only the plus-root, one-particle component. The first-chaos coefficient of the sine is $\mathbb E[G\sin(2\theta G)]=2\theta e^{-2\theta^2}$, so $$ \mathsf L^*v=2\theta s e^{-2\theta^2}e,\qquad \operatorname{Re}\langle v,\mathsf Lv\rangle =2\theta sc e^{-2\theta^2} =\theta e^{-2\theta^2}\sin(4\beta). $$ Here $\operatorname{Re}\langle e,v\rangle=c$ supplies the final factor. Thus the observable, not just the Gaussian law, agrees in all three representations. The example uses the [ordinary root updates][q-ordinary-updates] and [root shift][q-root-energy]. It calibrates one depth; the higher-depth occupation and replacement hypotheses remain necessary.
