passages.text: ### 8.2 Finite regularisation and the calculus needed for compilation Fix $T,N$ first. The independent continuous rounding coordinate makes the event at the sign discontinuity null. Bounded continuous odd approximations to that sign therefore converge in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. If the bounded output is $m^*$, shrink it to $(1-\kappa)m^*$, with fixed $0<\kappa<1$, before taking $\theta_\kappa=\tfrac12\arcsin((1-\kappa)m^*)$. This margin keeps the derivative of inverse sine bounded on its used range; the output loss is at most $\kappa$ in $L^2$. Then truncate the transmitted functions and approximate the resulting bounded maps by trigonometric polynomials. The source makes these choices from output toward leaves: each outer Lipschitz function is fixed before its inputs are approximated. The Gaussian isometry above converts an error in a transmitted child vector into the same $L^2$ error in its receiving position. Energy continuity then bounds the accumulated loss. The bounded output has the form $m=\sin(2\theta)$; it is the transmitted columns that are bounded, while the Gaussian fields themselves remain unbounded. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, bounded trigonometric approximation][q-bounded-classical]. **The formulas to be synthesized.** A mask is an event in the local seed space invariant under seed reversal. Fix a finite partition into masks, and write $p_R$ for the probability of mask $R$; probabilities used as denominators are positive. For disjoint masks $R,S$, aggregation on the finite regular tree means $$ (A_{RS}f)_i=\mathbf1_R(i)D^{-1/2} \sum_{j\sim i}\mathbf1_S(j)f_j. $$ A formula has a finite expression tree, with bounded measurable functions of the local seed as leaves. Internal operations are such aggregations or pointwise functions of previously formed quantities. Pointwise functions are smooth in their aggregate arguments, with polynomial bounds on all derivatives, uniformly in the seed. Seed dependence itself need not be smooth. Transmitted quantities are odd under simultaneous seed reversal; sent nonlinear functions and output angles are bounded, while aggregate Gaussian fields may be unbounded. An aggregation from $S$ to $R$ excludes $R$ if its transmitted formula uses no vertex of type $R$ below that call. All ancestor exclusions are retained, so a mask cannot recur on one active expression branch. It may recur on a different branch, and distinct branches may share descendants; exclusion asserts no independence between them. Gate targets are likewise excluded from the cross-edge dependencies of their parameters. This makes the physical all-neighbour calculation agree with the intended descendant calculation. For synthesis, reserve disjoint helper masks of positive mass, one per positive aggregation depth, absent from the output dependencies; the bounded odd output angle vanishes on their union. [OpenAI (2026b), Definition 3.3][q-formula-definition]; [Theorem 4.1][q-synthesis-statement]. The types can be encoded together with a Gaussian seed in one raw Gaussian variable: its sign supplies the odd symmetry, while disjoint binary digits of a uniform transform of its absolute value supply independent coordinates. The resulting finite type label is even and the Gaussian seed is odd under reversal. The associated pullback preserves vacuum, parity and $\mathsf L$. Thus adding types preserves the energy identification, rather than assuming an additional circuit resource. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, colours, exclusions and helpers][q-colors]. For the already fixed formula, the exclusion estimate is $$ \|m^{\rm col}-m\|^2\le C(\alpha+p_H), $$ where $\alpha$ is the largest nonhelper type mass and $p_H$ is the total helper mass. Its constant is independent of the number of types. The proof uses orthogonality of the disjoint masks before applying the Lipschitz estimate in the original, fixed list of formula coordinates. Treating the refined types as an arbitrary growing list of independent arguments would not provide this bound. The resulting classical near-optimality proposition supplies a finite bounded odd formula, zero on helpers, with energy as close to $P_*$ as required. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, “Type exclusion at small cost” and “Classical near-optimality in synthesis form”][q-colors]. **Which convergence permits the later substitutions?** The gate calculus uses recursive weights $\mathsf W_{h+1}=\mathsf W_0+d\Gamma(\Lambda_h)$, where $\Lambda_h$ is the previous weight restricted to the centred child space. The local weight includes the unbounded raw seed when needed. Its smooth domain is the intersection of all weighted domains. Smooth bounds mean polynomial bounds, with a finite loss of weight powers, for the maps, their adjoints and every specified parameter derivative. The finite height, fixed expression and fixed number of channels matter in these estimates. Strong convergence together with uniform stronger weighted bounds gives convergence in each weaker weighted norm by a spectral cutoff. This is the topology in which one replaces a gate inside a fixed surrounding circuit. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, weights and the topology of convergence][q-weights]. More precisely, the imported smooth-convergence contract is: for each output power $m$ and parameter multi-index $\alpha$, there are an input power $r$, exponent $k$ and constant $C$ such that $$ \|\mathsf W_D^m\partial_x^\alpha F_D(x)\xi\| \le C(1+|x|)^k\|\mathsf W_D^r\xi\|, \qquad \xi\in\bigcap_{q\ge0}\operatorname{Dom}(\mathsf W_D^q). $$ The bound is uniform in degree $D$ and parameter $x$. The same bound and strong convergence on smooth inputs are required for the adjoints and all specified parameter derivatives, with compatible limiting adjoints. Constants may depend on the fixed expression, height, channel list and derivative order. Bounded adjoint derivatives alone do not supply their convergence. At bounded local seeds $\mathsf W_0=1$; for polynomial Gaussian growth the source uses the vacuum-preserving weight $P_0+Q_0(1+|s|)Q_0$, where $P_0$ projects to the local vacuum and $Q_0=1-P_0$. These recursive weights control every generation. They differ from the top-generation number weight in §8.4's packet argument. No uniformity in growing word length, vanishing helper mass or the later seed-removal parameter is implicit in this contract. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth-family bound][q-weights]. One of the essential inputs retains a term beyond the Gaussian field. Let $K_D(x)$ be a smooth unitary family with $K_D(0)=1$, uniformly controlled derivatives and adjoint derivatives that converge smoothly in the stated weighted topology to those of a limiting family $K$, and centred first vacuum derivatives. Write $K_\alpha=\partial_\alpha K(0)=iT_\alpha$ and $K_{\alpha\lambda}=\partial_\alpha\partial_\lambda K(0)$. For a fixed finite parameter list $a$, the source proves $$ K_D(a/\sqrt D)^{\otimes D}\longrightarrow \exp\!\left\{ i\sum_\alpha a_\alpha q(T_\alpha\mathrm{vac}) +\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda}a_\alpha a_\lambda \left\langle K_{\alpha\lambda} +\tfrac12\{T_\alpha,T_\lambda\}\right\rangle_0 \right\}. $$ The second term is imaginary by unitarity. It survives because a second-order change of size $D^{-1}$ occurs in each of $D$ children. Its scalar coefficients become a possibly nonconstant controlled operator when commuting signals replace $a$. For example, $K(x)=e^{ix^2}$ has zero first derivative at zero but $K(a/\sqrt D)^D=e^{ia^2}$ exactly. Keeping only the first derivative would miss even this elementary contribution. The example explains why the term is necessary; the source's weighted product lemma supplies the general convergence and domain bounds. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Products of small unitaries”][q-unitary]. Commuting substitution is justified through a joint spectral calculus and Fourier estimates. It requires the physical control algebra, the self-adjoint signal operators and receiving seed to strongly commute, with joint exponential and weighted derivative bounds as stated in the source. This is stronger than a formal commutator identity on one domain. It does not require a nonsingular covariance matrix or an inverse Gram matrix. Exclusions establish that commuting algebra before a preceding circuit is conjugated through it; conjugation preserves commutation even when the signals share descendants. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Smooth commuting substitution”][q-substitution]. The exact cut recursion records the effect of such shared lower calculations. Let $y$ be the incoming boundary data, $V(y)$ the root matrix, and $m(y)$ its outgoing signals in the current frame. Factoring out the operations wholly inside each child gives $$ E^{[d]}(y)=V(y)\prod_{j\ \mathrm{child}} K_j^{[d-1]}(D^{-1/2}m(y)),\qquad K^{[d]}(y)=u^*E^{[d]}(0)^*E^{[d]}(y)u. $$ Every ratio $K^{[d]}$ equals one at zero. Nevertheless $m(0)$ generally does not vanish, because removing the parent input leaves the root's own signals. The actual zero-boundary root update is $u_{\rm new}=E^{[d]}(0)u$. It is not recovered by setting the entire ratio to one and discarding the baseline operation. Applying the unitary product lemma to this recursion, and then commuting substitution, is the source's smooth gate calculus. Its replacement statement covers a fixed finite surrounding sequence and its required parameter derivatives; it does not assert uniformity for arbitrary sequences whose length or channel count grows. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth gate calculus and its cut recursion][q-gate-calculus].

passages.text: ### 8.3 Seeded synthesis: helper contraction and nested responses Temporarily add longitudinal seed gates $\exp(-it\sum_i s_iZ_i)$, using an independent Gaussian $s_i$ at each vertex and reusing that same variable whenever a later seed gate acts there. The synthesis theorem turns the finite classical formula into a finite word of these gates, costs and mixers. Its ideal local $Y$ rotations have $Z$ insertion $$ v_{\rm cl}=|+\rangle m+|-\rangle n,\qquad m=\sin(2\theta). $$ Here $n$ is the remaining seed-dependent coefficient of the $|-\rangle$ component, not the number of spins. Both coefficients may depend on descendant seeds. The second term does not contribute to $\mathcal E$: $\mathsf L$ puts the root spin in $|+\rangle$, and shifting the $|-\rangle$ term puts a spin excitation into a child, orthogonal to the classical sector. Thus $\mathcal E(v_{\rm cl})=\mathcal E(m)$. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, classical rotations][q-root-energy] [OpenAI (2026b), §4, “Classical synthesis”][q-synthesis-statement]. There are two different approximation operations. First, seed conjugations of $X$ generate $\cos(2ts)X$ and $\sin(2ts)Y$. Trigonometric approximation and matrix commutators give the required bounded measurable masked spin controls. Sign averaging of masked $X$ flips isolates an interaction between chosen types; the cost terms commute, so this isolation is exact. This sign averaging is the refocusing method of [Jones and Knill (1999), §II, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9905008v1): orthogonal sign rows cancel unwanted Ising couplings, while identical rows retain a selected coupling. The source applies it to the finite partition of seed masks. Finite commutator products then approximate the desired pointwise matrices with smooth bounds. They can be substituted after the surrounding circuit has been fixed. The local masks are measurable functions of the seed; smoothness is required in the continuous aggregate inputs, not in the mask labels. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, elementary masked controls and matrix products][q-masked-controls]. The second operation implements an aggregation. Let $I$ be the receiver region, $J$ the sender region, and $K$ an unused helper region of fixed positive probability $p_K$. They are disjoint. The lower seed-only formula $f$ excludes these regions along its cross-edge paths. With $A_{ij}=D^{-1/2}1_{i\sim j}$, the desired propagation has generator $$ H=\sum_{i\in I,j\in J}P_iA_{ij}f_j. $$ Partition $J$ into parts $J_l$ of probabilities $p_l$. Two levels of spin commutators generate the commuting Hamiltonian $$ \widetilde H_{\mathcal P} =\frac1{p_K}\sum_l\sum_{i\in I,\,j,j'\in J_l,\,k\in K} P_iA_{ij}X_jA_{jk}X_kA_{kj'}X_{j'}f_{j'}. $$ For a fixed receiver–sender edge $i\sim j$, the terms with $j=j'$ contain $X_j^2=1$; $f_j$ is seed-only and commutes with these spin factors. On helper-pinned states $X_k=1$, so their sum is exactly $$ \frac1{p_K}P_iA_{ij}f_j \sum_{k\in K}A_{jk}A_{kj} =P_iA_{ij}f_j\frac{N_K(j)}{Dp_K}, $$ where $N_K(j)$ counts helper neighbours of $j$. Conditional on the receiver edge, its endpoint $i\in I$ is not a helper and the other $D$ neighbours have mean helper count $Dp_K$. Its binomial variance is $Dp_K(1-p_K)$, so the ratio tends to one in $L^2$ at fixed $p_K>0$. Terms with $j\ne j'$ are simple paths and must disappear under partition refinement. The factor $1/p_K$ is harmless only after a positive helper mass has been fixed. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, helper generators and contraction][q-helper-statement]. Helper pinning is a statement about every helper spin in the light cone. Its finite-degree projection is $$ \Pi_{K,V}=\prod_{v\in V} \left[1-1_K(s_v)\frac{1-X_v}{2}\right]. $$ It retains the seed variables and helper-labelled descendant spaces while fixing the helper spins in $|+\rangle$. The ideal propagation, the exact Hamiltonian $\widetilde H_{\mathcal P}$, and the surrounding gates that avoid $K$ preserve this compressed space. Multiplying an insertion by $1_{K^c}(s_o)$ only masks the root label and does not impose this descendant condition. Individual finite commutator factors may leave the compressed space. Accordingly, the proof first establishes the exact contraction there, then chooses finite commutator products on the full space to approximate it. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, “Simultaneous helper contraction”][q-helper-statement]. The estimate controlling a growing partition is $$ \rho^2=\sum_l p_l^2\le p_J\max_l p_l\longrightarrow0. $$ At a helper root, each part supplies two commuting fields with columns $d_l,e_l$ on disjoint sender masks, of weighted norm at most $C\sqrt{p_l}$. The remaining correction is a sum of centred quadratics $$ \sum_l\bigl[q(d_l)q(e_l)-\langle d_l,e_l\rangle\bigr]. $$ Normal ordering and disjoint-mask orthogonality bound its quadratic kernels by $C\rho$ in Hilbert–Schmidt norm. The source separately bounds the exponentials in the weighted topology, uniformly in the number of parts. Smallness of the generator on smooth vectors alone would not justify inserting its exponential into the surrounding circuit. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, “Quadratics with many orthogonal columns”][q-helper-quadratics]. The helper estimate alone does not control all cuts. Put $\epsilon_{\mathcal P}=\max_l\sqrt{p_l}$. The receiver and helper corrections have weighted size $O(\rho)$; a sender correction is $O(\sqrt{p_l})$ conditional on its label. The remaining lower-formula responses have size $O(\epsilon_{\mathcal P})$. Both quantities tend to zero with $f$, the number of lower channels and $p_K>0$ fixed. There remains a response inside the lower formula $f$. A cut can pass through a descendant used to compute $f$, rather than through one of the displayed three-edge paths. The source first writes the exact difference of the affected Hamiltonian terms before applying the preceding subtree circuit. That circuit is fixed with respect to the new cut input. Exclusions ensure that the downward coefficients are independent of that active boundary argument. The resulting additive cut-response rule retains both first derivatives and mixed second derivatives: $$ \sum_\alpha a_\alpha q(H_\alpha\mathrm{vac}) +\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda}a_\alpha a_\lambda \langle H_{\alpha\lambda}\rangle_0. $$ Here $H_\alpha$ is centred by parity; no limit of the extensive zero-input Hamiltonian is required. The self-adjoint generator is obtained from the limiting time group of cut ratios. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Additive cut responses”][q-additive-response]. After substituting the signals of a lower formula, a boundary difference contains, in particular, $$ \begin{aligned} &\sum_\alpha[m_\alpha(y)-m_\alpha(0)]q(r_\alpha)\\ &\quad+\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda} [m_\alpha(y)m_\lambda(y)-m_\alpha(0)m_\lambda(0)] c_{\alpha\lambda}. \end{aligned} $$ The mixed coefficients $c_{\alpha\lambda}$ must remain even when two channels share descendants. A bounded scalar example makes the issue visible: for a shared standard normal $Q$, take $H(y_1,y_2)=\cos(Q+y_1+y_2)-\cos Q$. At zero both first derivatives are $-\sin Q$ and are centred, but $\mathbb E H_{12}=-e^{-1/2}$. The two cross terms in the half-sum therefore contribute $-e^{-1/2}a_1a_2$. Centred first responses do not remove a mixed second response. This example checks the algebraic reason for retaining the term; the cut-response theorem supplies the operator and domain justification. At the actual root there is no parent input to subtract: the corresponding unsubtracted $m(0)$ terms enter the root update. The source propagates small terminal responses through the fixed depth and fixed list of lower channels. It refines the calling sender mask while keeping those lower formulas fixed. This is what controls all cuts in a simultaneous replacement of several calls. A root-seed scalar phase may remain on helper labels; it cancels in insertions and child conjugations. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, lower-formula responses and completion of the contraction proof][q-helper-responses]. Compilation now proceeds from outer aggregations to inner ones. Reserve a separate unused helper type for each aggregation rank. At a given rank, establish the simultaneous exact contraction, fix the sender partitions, and only then choose finite commutator approximations. Subsequent inner calls use their own helpers, which remain unused. Each inner accuracy is chosen after its surrounding finite sequence is fixed. This order avoids assuming uniformity over all helper masses, ranks or circuit lengths. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, order of compilation][q-compilation]. If the resulting insertion $v$ obeys $\|1_{H^c}(v-v_{\rm cl})\|<\eta$, seed commutation and unitarity give $\|1_Hv\|=\sqrt{p_H}$. First omit the helper part of $v$, at energy cost at most $2\sqrt{p_H}$. Compare the two insertions projected off helpers; their norm difference is below $\eta$, so their energies differ by at most $2\eta$. The projected classical insertion still has energy $\mathcal E(m)$ because $m=0$ on helpers. Thus $$ |\mathcal E(v)-\mathcal E(m)|\le2\eta+2\sqrt{p_H}. $$ All projected insertion vectors have norm at most one. This completes the interface from a bounded classical formula to a finite seeded word. It uses the source's smooth gate and helper-contraction theorems; it is not a consequence of the scalar theorem or of a finite-degree central limit theorem alone. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, synthesis statement and its proof][q-synthesis-statement].

passages.text: ### 8.4 Removing the seed controls without changing their joint law Seed removal must simulate one Gaussian variable per vertex, reused at all seed gates. Replacing each occurrence with a fresh independent Gaussian would change the circuit. The source proves a theorem for any already fixed finite seeded word and any energy tolerance, producing one finite ordinary word. Its proof works in the fixed-word tree limit; it does not take a degree limit simultaneously with its small parameter. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, “Removal of seed controls”][q-seed-statement]. **A small component supplies a large response.** Fix $b>0$ and $01$. The right side is $o(r)$: within each ordinary packet the relevant Hermitian expectation is real, distinct packet centres have overlap $O(r^M)$, and terms containing only special packets have size $O(r^2)$. The norm remainder is carried by unitarity; it receives no unproved occupation bound. The exact zero clocks then cancel the first-order displacement on ordinary packets, leaving $o(r)$ error there. The prescribed action on a normalized special packet has $o(1)$ error, multiplied by its $O(r)$ amplitude. These are the unequal accuracy requirements that the next echo uses. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, accuracy of selective probes][q-seed-selective]. **The echo amplifies a controlled difference.** Consider a forward cost $t/r$, a selective flip of the special component, the reverse cost $-t/r$, and a selective undoing of that flip. The packet invariant transports the special component so that its contribution to the insertion changes sign. For the actual insertion directions before and after the first flip, it gives $$ v'_r-v_r=-2r\,w_r+o(r). $$ The Weyl product of the two costs is formed with these actual directions before making any approximation. Their large centres cancel, leaving a bounded displacement $$ \frac tr(v'_r-v_r)=-2t\,w_r+o(1). $$ Approximating each direction by a low component with merely $O(r)$ error before this subtraction would leave an uncontrolled order-one error. The remaining scalar Weyl phase is independent of the root spin and cancels in insertions; it need not itself converge. The second flip restores the transported special component so that the same construction can be used again. Mixers receive analogous selective compensations. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, packet invariant, insertion approximation and “One echo”][q-seed-echo]. In the limit, $\ell_r$ and $w_r$ become two orthogonal external real Gaussian modes at each root. The initialization uses $q(\ell)$ and every simulated seed gate uses the same $q(w)$: choosing $t=\sigma/2$ implements $e^{-i\sigma Zq(w)}$. Different vertices have independent local copies. This is the required joint law of the seeded word. A finite induction uses the Weyl identity $$ \langle W(f)\Omega,W(g)\Omega\rangle =\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\|g-f\|^2 +i\operatorname{Im}\langle f,g\rangle\right) $$ to match the relevant finite Gram matrices. Escaping high directions supply precisely the vanishing pairings between the new external modes and endogenous child directions. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, external-mode limit][q-seed-gram]. **The energy pairing after seed removal.** Matching the seed law and its finite Gram matrices is not yet enough. For a centred low insertion $h=\sum_j s_j\otimes W(f_j)\Omega$, the one-particle coefficient of $W(f_j)\Omega$ is $i e^{-\|f_j\|^2/2}f_j$. Hence $$ \langle h,\mathsf Lh\rangle =-i\sum_j\langle s_j,+\rangle e^{-\|f_j\|^2/2} \langle f_j,h\rangle. $$ In the seeded representation, $\mathsf L$ places the root-seed factor in its vacuum and creates $h$ only in the endogenous child space. External components therefore contribute zero to the last pairing. The high-direction estimate yields the same zeros in the actual limit. The actual insertion differs from its low insertion by $O(r)$, so energy continuity completes the comparison. Matching Gram matrices without this one-particle calculation would not identify $\mathsf L$ or its energy. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, “Finite Gram induction,” including the energy calculation][q-seed-gram]. **Why the selective rotations are available at every required stage.** The limiting projection of each special centre must be nonzero. The source imposes finitely many visibility conditions on the angles of the formal seeded word. At each relevant standard stage they have form $$ -2\operatorname{Im}\langle v_Z^{\rm form}, -2bz\,e+yD^{\rm form}\rangle\ne0, \qquad z,y\in\{\pm1\}, $$ where $e=Z\mathrm{vac}$ and $D^{\rm form}$ accumulates echoes whose reverse costs have already occurred. These functions are real analytic by the finite Weyl formulas. Setting all target angles to zero, while retaining initialization, gives $4bz e^{-8b^2}\ne0$, so none is identically zero. An arbitrarily small angle perturbation avoids their finite union of zero sets and the zero echo-time hyperplanes. The huge-cost stages need a separate transverse-projection estimate; their limiting projection pairs then also have a nonzero coordinate. Finite pulse lists can now be chosen successively from limits already established at earlier stages. No list is chosen from a limit that assumes its own successful implementation. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, huge-stage transverse projection, visibility and construction order][q-seed-visibility]. The choices are therefore nested: make $b$ small to control initialization; perturb the fixed target angles to ensure visibility; choose all finite probe lists; finally choose $r$ small. A value of $r$ fixes every large angle and every finite product. The theorem allows those angles to be large or negative. It makes no claim of uniform bounds as the target word length grows or as the tolerance tends to zero. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, proof of seed removal][q-seed-visibility].

passages.text: ### 9.1 Smoothness of the minimizing coefficient Full support does not by itself prove that the Stieltjes measure has a density. In the source manuscript, that conclusion uses the PDE again after the gap contradiction has established $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$. We reconstruct the additional argument here because it explains a further conclusion of the original paper. It is not a clause of the selected full-support formal statement. Put $f_k=\partial_x^k\Phi_\gamma$, so $f_1=u$ and $f_2=a$. All formulas in this subsection are on a fixed compact time strip, where every finite collection of spatial derivatives is bounded. Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's formula along the associated diffusion gives $$ df_k(t,X_t)= -\frac{\gamma(t)}2\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\binom{k}{j} f_{j+1}(t,X_t)f_{k-j+1}(t,X_t)\,dt +f_{k+1}(t,X_t)\,dB_t. $$ The sum is empty when $k=1$. This identity needs no derivative of $\gamma$. For an initially nonsmooth coefficient, apply it to finite-step approximations and pass to the integrated identity: the coefficient converges in $L^1$, the spatial factors converge uniformly, and the stochastic integrals converge by the Itô isometry. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, smooth-density proof, lines 35–50][fs-density]. Set $b=f_3$. The case $k=2$ gives $da=-\gamma a^2dt+b\,dB_t$, and consequently $$ 0=\frac d{dt}\mathbb E a^2 =\mathbb E b^2-2\gamma(t)\mathbb E a^3 \quad\text{for almost every }t<1. $$ Convexity gives $a\geq0$; the already established second moment gives $\mathbb E a^3\geq(\mathbb E a^2)^{3/2}=1$. Thus the quotient $$ \widetilde\gamma(t)=\frac{\mathbb E b(t,X_t)^2} {2\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^3} $$ is well defined and continuous, before any continuity of $\gamma$ is known. It equals $\gamma$ almost everywhere. Approaching an arbitrary $t<1$ from the right through the full-measure equality set, continuity of $\widetilde\gamma$ and right continuity of $\gamma$ give equality at that $t$ as well. This proves continuity of $\gamma$. At zero, $X_0=0$, and evenness of $\Phi(0,\cdot)$ gives $b(0,0)=0$; hence $\gamma(0)=0$. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, lines 52–66][fs-density]; [Chen, Proposition 4.6, pp. 25–26][chen26]. The bootstrap must treat all polynomial moments simultaneously. For a polynomial $P$ in finitely many variables, write $$ M_P(t)=\mathbb E P(f_1(t,X_t),\ldots,f_m(t,X_t)). $$ The preceding stochastic identities and Itô's product rule provide polynomials $Q_P,R_P$, involving only finitely many additional derivatives, such that $$ M_P(t)-M_P(0)=\int_0^t\bigl(M_{Q_P}(s)+\gamma(s)M_{R_P}(s)\bigr)\,ds. $$ Explicitly, if $$ D_k(y)=-\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\binom{k}{j}y_{j+1}y_{k-j+1}, $$ then $$ Q_P=\tfrac12\sum_{k,l}\partial_{kl}P\,y_{k+1}y_{l+1}, \qquad R_P=\sum_k\partial_kP\,D_k. $$ All these moments start continuous. Once $\gamma$ is continuous, the integral formula makes every moment $C^1$, and the quotient formula makes $\gamma$ itself $C^1$. If all moments and $\gamma$ are $C^r$, the same argument makes them $C^{r+1}$. Induction proves $\gamma\in C^\infty([0,1))$, with derivatives at zero taken from the right. Since $\gamma(0)=0$, there is no atom at zero; its Stieltjes measure is $\gamma'(t)\,dt$, and monotonicity gives $\gamma'\geq0$. This is the polynomial-moment method credited by the source to Auffinger–Chen and to Chen's zero-temperature treatment. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, lines 68–101][fs-density]; [Auffinger and Chen, proof of Theorem 2(ii), p. 16][ac-properties]; [Chen, Appendix B.6, p. 38][chen26]. The identity $d(a^2)=(-2\gamma a^3+b^2)dt+2ab\,dB$ requires the cube used above; the moment induction itself is unchanged.

Choose one minimizer supplied by the attained Parisi formula, and apply

theorem below then applies at every point of its Stieltjes support. For every fixed $r\in[0,1)$ and $\varepsilon,\eta>0$,
there is a constant $K=K(r,\varepsilon,\eta)>0$, independent of $n$, such that
$$
\mathbb P\left(\exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n:
\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i\tau_i-r\right|<\varepsilon,
\quad \frac{H_n(\sigma)}n,\frac{H_n(\tau)}n\ge P_*-\eta\right)
\ge1-Ke^{-n/K},\qquad n\ge1.
$$
The probability is over the SK couplings; the configurations may depend on
them. This is the specialization of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1,
equation (5), p. 5][acz] to the full-support minimizer above. Their theorem
applies to each point of its Stieltjes support. Its proof, on pp. 15–16,
uses the coupled free energy constrained to a neighbourhood of that
overlap, passes to the coupled maximum and applies Gaussian concentration.
The coupled maximum approaches $2P_*$, while the unrestricted maximum
approaches $P_*$; these two facts force both members of a maximizing pair
to be near ground energy.

The covariance normalization needs one small adjustment. Writing
$R=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$, our Hamiltonian has covariance
$nR^2/2-1/2$. Adjoin a common independent Gaussian $C$ of variance $1/2$.
Then $\widetilde H_n(\sigma)=H_n(\sigma)+C$ has covariance
$n\xi(R)$ with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, as in the cited mixed-spin theorem.
Its expected maximum equals that of $H_n$, so its ground-state limit is
the same $P_*$. Apply the theorem with energy tolerance $\eta/2$.
On $|C|\le\eta n/2$, the resulting pair also satisfies the displayed
energy inequalities for $H_n$. The omitted event has probability at most
$2e^{-\eta^2n^2/4}$, which can be absorbed into $Ke^{-n/K}$ by enlarging
$K$. Since the conclusion for $H_n$ depends only on its couplings,
this also removes the auxiliary Gaussian from the probability statement.

The pointwise result also gives a simultaneous statement at any fixed
positive resolution. Given $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, choose finitely many
centres $r_j\in[0,1)$ whose open $\varepsilon/2$-neighbourhoods cover
$[0,1]$. Apply the preceding result at each centre with overlap tolerance
$\varepsilon/2$ and energy tolerance $\eta$. A finite union bound gives
constants $C,c>0$, depending only on these tolerances, such that
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\forall r\in[-1,1]\ \exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n:
 |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon,\quad
 H_n(\sigma)/n,H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta\right)
 \ge1-Ce^{-cn}.
\tag{9.1}
$$
Indeed, on the event where every centre has a suitable pair, choose a
nearest centre and use the triangle inequality. For negative targets,
reverse one spin configuration: the pure two-spin Hamiltonian preserves
its energy and changes the overlap's sign. The finite net covers the
endpoints as well, with centres strictly below one.

This deduction uses fixed tolerances and target-dependent pairs. It gives
neither exact arbitrary real overlaps at finite $n$, a typical-pair law,
a search procedure, nor a guarantee for tolerances shrinking with $n$.
It uses the external landscape theorem, full support and attainment, and
is outside the two selected formal statements in §12. The separate
algorithmic consequence is in §9.4.

### 11.1.2 Finite-temperature values and exact Gibbs samples

This comparison samples the exact Gibbs distribution. The QAOA Born law
in §11.2 is a separate distribution; none of the following bounds identifies
the two. For one fixed instance, let $L_n=\max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)/n$,
$\mathcal F_{n,\beta}=(n\beta)^{-1}\log\sum_\sigma e^{\beta H_{n,J}(\sigma)}$,
and let $\mathcal U_{n,\beta}$ be the mean energy per spin under the
Gibbs law proportional to $e^{\beta H_{n,J}(\sigma)}$. Then
$$
0\le\mathcal F_{n,\beta}-L_n\le\frac{\log2}{\beta},\qquad
0\le L_n-\mathcal U_{n,\beta}\le\frac{\log2}{\beta}.
$$
The first is the log-sum bound. The second uses
$\mathcal F=\mathcal U+S/(n\beta)$, where the Gibbs entropy satisfies
$0\le S\le n\log2$, together with $\mathcal U\le L_n\le\mathcal F$.
Thus both disorder averages approach $P_*$ along every joint
$n\to\infty$, $\beta\to\infty$, by the already established
convergence of $\mathbb E L_n$.

There is also a finite probability estimate. Every configuration has
Gaussian coefficient-vector norm $\sqrt{(n-1)/(2n^2)}$ after division
by $n$, and their maximum has the same Lipschitz bound. Gaussian
concentration gives, for $n\ge2$,
$$
\Pr_J(|L_n-\mathbb E L_n|>s)
\le2\exp\{-n^2s^2/(n-1)\}.
$$
For an exact Gibbs draw $\Sigma^{\rm G}$, count the at most $2^n$
configurations with deficit at least $s$ and bound the partition sum
below by its maximal term. This gives, for every instance,
$$
\Pr\{H_{n,J}(\Sigma^{\rm G})/n\le L_n-s\mid J\}
\le\min\{1,e^{n(\log2-\beta s)}\}.
$$
The lower tail below $P_*-s$ is bounded by
$\Pr_J(L_n<P_*-s/2)+\min\{1,e^{n(\log2-\beta s/2)}\}$;
the upper tail is at most the upper tail of $L_n$. Hence an exact
Gibbs sample also approaches $P_*$ in joint probability. These are
elementary scalar consequences of the Gibbs law, entropy and Gaussian
concentration. They supply neither an efficient sampler nor QAOA angles.

First the couplings $J$ are sampled; then a computational-basis measurement of the state produces a spin string $\Sigma$. For the single word $W$ already chosen, put $$ E_n(J,\Sigma)=H_{n,J}(\Sigma)/n,\qquad \overline E_n(J)=\mathbb E[E_n(J,\Sigma)\mid J]. $$ The quantity defining $v_W$ is $\mathbb E_J\overline E_n(J)$. It is neither the energy of every measured string nor a worst-disorder guarantee. The temporary Gaussian labels used during synthesis are not an extra source of randomness in the final angle vectors. passages.text: ### 11.3 Depth, angle choice and the order of quantifiers The complete witness is a finite ordered word, including every real angle. Its existence for each error tolerance asserts uniformity in system size and disorder that fixed-instance convergence does not provide. The quantifiers should be read literally. The source theorem says that for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is one finite word $W_\varepsilon$ such that $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E E_n(W_\varepsilon)\ge P_*-\varepsilon. $$ The cost operator uses $J,n$, but this word and its angles do not. In fixed-instance QAOA convergence, by contrast, the chosen depth and angles may depend on the fixed finite cost matrix and the requested accuracy. The performance of a prescribed family of nonzero angles with $p=p(n)\to\infty$ needs further estimates. A depth allowance alone can be met by the padded existence construction below. The distinction already occurs for the elementary array $a_{n,p}=p/(n+p)$. For each fixed $n$, its limit as $p\to\infty$ is one; for each fixed $p$, its limit as $n\to\infty$ is zero. This is a quantifier example, not a model of QAOA. The finite-dimensional convergence theorem of [Binkowski, Koßmann, Ziegler and Schwonnek, arXiv:2302.04968v1, Theorem 12][binkowski] fixes the optimization problem before selecting a sufficiently long circuit. It does not replace the construction of a size-independent word here. **An existential schedule under a prescribed depth allowance.** There is a narrower diagonal consequence for sampled output. Choose $W_k$ with $P_*-1/k\le v_{W_k}\le P_*$. Fixed-word second-moment convergence supplies $N_k$ so that, for every $n\ge N_k$, $\mathbb E(E_n(W_k)-v_{W_k})^2\le k^{-2}$. Given any prescribed integer depth allowance $d(n)\to\infty$, enlarge these strictly increasing thresholds until $d(n)\ge\operatorname{depth}(W_k)$ for every $n\ge N_k$. On $N_k\le n **Computational meaning of a finite word.** Nor does a supremum over angles assert that an optimizing angle vector exists at any particular depth. The proof constructs a sufficiently good word directly; monotonicity from identity padding then gives the limit of $Q_p$. Each QAOA round contains a full cost evolution and a mixer evolution. In the dense SK model a cost evolution involves all $\binom n2$ pair couplings, so the round count is not itself a bound on two-qubit gate depth, connectivity cost, precision or physical runtime. Three computational questions remain distinct. Evaluating the limiting energy at supplied angles is one task; finding suitable angles is another; implementing and sampling the resulting quantum circuit is a third. The [Basso et al. iteration][bfmvz] evaluates the fixed-angle limit in $O(p^2 4^p)$ arithmetic time. That is not a bound on the search needed to find the existence theorem's angles. Spin–boson representations provide another route to evaluation. The earlier [Boulebnane et al. mapping, arXiv:2505.07929v2][spin-boson], and the later [mixed-spin decoupling paper, arXiv:2609.40309v1, §§II–III and Supplement S2.1][decoupling], must be distinguished: the latter is a separate work, not the reference called BKL2026 in the original QAOA manuscript. Its fixed-depth mapping and numerical tensor-network performance do not supply an efficient angle-selection theorem for the present construction. Its discussion also gives fixed-word finite-size estimates; the absence of a finite-size rate **in the construction here** is not a claim that the wider literature contains none. **Why the two-spin hypothesis matters.** The statement is specific to the quadratic, zero-field SK model. The pure even higher-spin model has a different thermodynamic-first conclusion. For every even interaction order $q\ge4$, [Basso, Gamarnik, Mei and Zhou, arXiv:2204.10306v2, Theorem 4, (3.15), and its proof in §4.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.10306v2) show $$ v_p^{(q)}(\boldsymbol\theta,\boldsymbol\beta) \le\eta_{\mathrm{OGP}}(G_q)<\eta_{\mathrm{OPT}}(G_q) $$ for every finite $p$ and every fixed angle vector, in that source's normalization. The same ceiling bounds their supremum over all finite $p$ and angles. The proof combines its dense–sparse value identity with the coupled-overlap-gap obstruction of [Chou, Love, Sandhu and Shi, arXiv:2108.06049v3, Parameter 4.1 and Corollary 4.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.06049v3). That local-algorithm obstruction applies to sparse random signed Max-$q$-XOR for even $q\ge4$, at sufficiently large fixed degree and under the source's logarithmic-depth bound. The Basso–Gamarnik–Mei–Zhou transfer above only needs the resulting obstruction at each fixed depth. It requires no interchange of depth and system size. The exclusion $q\ge4$ is essential; this is not an obstruction for the SK two-spin model treated here. For comparison, [Goh, arXiv:2404.06087v6, Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.2.1][goh], treats even interaction order at least four. Its logarithmic-depth obstruction concerns sparse random-regular Max-q-XORSAT; the dense spin-glass corollary is explicitly conditional on swapping limits. The source states on p. 12 that its sparse/dense equivalence is only established at fixed depth, so it does not prove a dense logarithmic-depth obstruction. These hypotheses do not include quadratic SK. Neither a conclusion for all mixed spin glasses nor a general quantum advantage follows from §8. ### 11.4 The regular-MaxCut consequence has its own limits The original manuscript also gives a consequence for MaxCut. For each $\eta>0$ it selects one finite depth and normalized angles, and then a degree threshold, such that every finite simple unweighted $(D+1)$-regular graph of girth greater than $2p+1$ has expected cut fraction at least $$ \frac12+\frac{P_*-\eta}{\sqrt D} $$ for all sufficiently large $D$. The usual MaxCut cost is $H_{\rm MC}=\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}}(I-Z_iZ_j)$, so its angles are $2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D$: the normalized angles are fixed, while these physical cost angles depend on degree. The sign conversion uses a bipartition of the relevant tree neighbourhood of each edge; the whole graph need not be bipartite. The further optimality comparison is for a uniform simple labelled $(D+1)$-regular graph $G_{n,D+1}$, along sizes with $n(D+1)$ even. Write $\operatorname{OPT}(G)$ for the maximum cut size divided by $|E(G)|$, $q_{p,G}$ for the circuit's expected cut fraction, and $\Delta_D(G)=\operatorname{OPT}(G)-q_{p,G}(2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D, \boldsymbol\beta)$. The same word can be chosen so that $$ \lim_{D\to\infty} \limsup_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n(D+1)\ \mathrm{even}}} \Pr_G\{\sqrt D\,\Delta_D(G_{n,D+1})>\eta\}=0. $$ Size goes to infinity first at fixed degree and word. The probability is over the random graph; the cut fraction has already averaged the quantum measurement. For fixed $D,p$, [McKay, Wormald and Wysocka (2004), Theorem 1](https://doi.org/10.37236/1819), gives tight counts of cycles of lengths at most $2p+3$. Every edge with a nontree neighbourhood is within bounded distance of one of these cycles, so their fraction tends to zero. The optimum is supplied separately by [Dembo, Montanari and Sen, arXiv:1503.03923v2, Theorem 1.6(b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03923v2): dividing their cut size per vertex by $(D+1)/2$ gives the leading cut fraction $1/2+P_*/\sqrt{D+1}$, with an error $o(D^{-1/2})$ in the stated iterated regime. A high-girth lower bound alone would not prove optimality on every high-girth graph. See [OpenAI (2026b), Corollary 1.2 and its complete proof][q-maxcut]. This separate consequence is recorded to preserve the source's scope; it is not a new selected formal endpoint or a joint size–degree limit.

passages.text: ### 11.5 A later finite-size estimate and its limited depth consequence A separate, later source gives a quantitative comparison with the fixed-angle limit. Boulebnane, Khan, Subrahmanya, Herman, Farhi, Villalonga and Shaydulin, [arXiv:2609.40309v1, Corollary S3.1, pp. 46–47][decoupling], use the ordered-tuple Gaussian mixed-spin cost with covariance polynomial $\xi(t)=\sum_q c_q^2t^q$ of finite degree. Let $\Gamma>0$ bound every cost angle in a depth-$p$ word. Choose $x>0$ bounding $\xi(2),\xi'(1),\xi''(33)$, with $\Gamma^2p^2x\ge1$. No bound on the mixer angles is needed. Set $$ B_p=256p^4(2e\Gamma^2p^2x)^p,\qquad E_p=70\Gamma^2p^2x+p\log2,\qquad R_p=(2E_p/\log2)^{2p}. $$ For $$ 0<\varepsilon\le4\Gamma px \min\{e^{-1/2},2^{-(8p^2+3)/100}\}, $$ the source asserts $|\nu_n-\nu_\infty|\le\varepsilon$ whenever $$ n\ge T_p:=\max\left\{ 2^{8p^2+3}B_p \left(\frac{2^{\deg\xi+4}\Gamma^2p^2x^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)^{R_p} \left[2\log_2\frac{4\Gamma px}{\varepsilon}+\deg\xi\right]^2, \frac{16\Gamma px}{\varepsilon}\right\}. $$ Here $\nu_n$ is the disorder-averaged energy per spin. The estimate applies to each near-optimal word from §8.6 separately. Given $\zeta>0$, choose a finite word $W_\zeta$ with $\nu_\infty(W_\zeta)\ge P_*-\zeta/2$. Its depth $p_\zeta$ and cost angles are finite; pad by a zero layer if needed and take $\Gamma_\zeta=\max\{1,\max_j|\theta_j(W_\zeta)|\}$. Choose a positive $\varepsilon_\zeta\le\zeta/2$ satisfying the displayed small-error condition. With these fixed parameters, the threshold gives $$ \nu_n(W_\zeta)\ge P_*-\zeta\qquad(n\ge T_{p_\zeta}). $$ The threshold is explicit in the chosen word and error. The existential construction supplies no quantitative bounds for $p_\zeta$ or $\Gamma_\zeta$ as $\zeta\downarrow0$, so it does not yield a bound in accuracy alone. A common angle bound is needed for the uniform growing-depth consequence below, not for this fixed-word application. For SK take $c_2=1/\sqrt2$. Combining the two ordered off-diagonal couplings recovers our standard Gaussian $J_{ij}$; the diagonal adds an independent scalar Gaussian of variance $1/2$. That scalar changes the circuit by a global phase and has zero mean, so the expected-energy comparison uses the same normalization. A fixed $x\ge\max\{2,\Gamma^{-2}\}$ satisfies the above bounds for every $p\ge1$. For fixed mixture, $\Gamma$ and $x$, put $\varepsilon_p=e^{-p^2}$. The small-error condition holds eventually, and direct logarithms give $$ \log R_p=4p\log p+O(p),\qquad \log\log T_p=4p\log p+O(p+\log p). $$ Consequently, for any deterministic sequence of words $W_n$ with depths $p(n)\to\infty$, one common cost-angle bound $\Gamma$, and $p(n)\log p(n)=o(\log\log n)$, the displayed hypotheses hold and $|\nu_n(W_n)-\nu_\infty(W_n)|\le e^{-p(n)^2}$ eventually. This is a uniform comparison along that specified bounded-angle class. It gives neither an efficient way to find near-optimal angles nor concentration of a quantum measurement in this growing-depth regime. The fixed-word second-moment theorem in §11.2 has separate quantifiers.

### 12.1 The support statement and the derivative bridge

The first formal statement assumes a Brownian system and an admissible
minimizer. It supplies a Stieltjes measure, an associated diffusion, full
relative support and strict increase, and the two moment identities for
every associated diffusion. Its proof assembles contact, exclusion of a
terminal plateau, curvature for positive and zero constant intervals,
and uniqueness to transfer the moments between associated diffusions.
This describes the inspected proof's mathematical route; no successful
research-target replay is claimed. Its quantifiers are
$\forall W\,\forall\gamma$, followed by the minimizer hypothesis;
it supplies both witnesses on the given Brownian system. The moment
conclusion is universal over every diffusion satisfying the specified
equation, and covers exactly $0\le t<1$. The diffusion equation itself
holds through time one, simultaneously for all those times outside
one null set. Controls are progressive for the natural filtration of
Brownian increments and bounded by one pointwise. These are not
additional regularity or minimizer-existence assumptions. See the
[exact support statement][support-type] and the companion
source-interface review.

There is one useful distinction between the manuscript's first variation
and its formal counterpart. The formal result initially gives a derivative
along chord lengths $1/(n+1)$. For this particular control functional,
that sampled limit determines the ordinary feasible right derivative.
With a control fixed, the terminal absolute value is convex in the
coefficient while the penalty is linear. The supremum over the same
control class, and then subtraction of the linear Parisi penalty,
preserve convexity. The secant slopes therefore vary monotonically as
the chord shortens; each intervening chord lies between two successive
sampled chords and has the same limiting slope. If $\eta$ is an
integrable feasible direction, choose $\varepsilon_0>0$ so that
$\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ is admissible and rescale the chord. This
bridge is an ordinary deduction from the definitions and sampled limit,
not an additional formally named theorem.

At the origin, the manuscript smoothly extends auxiliary quotient
variables. The formal coercivity proof for the spatial diffusion density instead works on the positive
half-line, controls the zero flux at the origin and reflects. What must
agree is the resulting integrated inequality; auxiliary values at zero
need not coincide. In particular, the declared generic flux lemma has
a global derivative hypothesis that is not the supplier used here:
the finite-density proof uses the Gaussian half-line coercivity lemma
and reflection. A totalized quotient value at zero cannot silently
satisfy the generic global hypothesis. The precise source spans are in
the correspondence record.
The [fixed-time supplier `actual_coercivity`][support-fixed-time] assumes
positive time and continuity of the coefficient at that time. Its scaled
polynomial inequality is (4.1) multiplied by $c^2$; division requires
$c>0$. This gives a direct source destination for Proposition 4.1 without
adding a minimizing or plateau premise.

passages.text: ### 12.3 Relating the two statements The support and scalar models encode closely related control problems. A direct formal application still needs a specified map of their objects. The following contract identifies the obligations, rather than asserting an equivalence of their complete interfaces. **Coefficients.** Restrict the scalar real-time coefficient to $[0,1)$; conversely, choose an extension compatible with the scalar right-continuity predicate. Prove equality almost everywhere of the coefficients used by each payoff and penalty. The scalar endpoint and exterior values are unconstrained by the shape conditions, so two extensions need not be literally equal. **Brownian space.** Bundle or unbundle the same sample space, sigma algebra, probability law and Brownian process. Identify the natural filtration and every elapsed-increment filtration. Equality in law alone does not identify admissible controls on a chosen space. **Controls and payoffs.** Bundle an admissible scalar control as a support control and conversely. With $s=t+r$, prove equality between the absolute integral over $[t,1]$ using $\alpha(s-t)$ and the elapsed integral over $[0,1-t]$ using $\alpha(r)$. Preserve progressive measurability and the pointwise bound $|\alpha|\le1$. **Value and minimizer.** Equality of the payoff sets gives equality of their suprema for every $x$ and $0\le t<1$. Only then identify the first and second spatial derivatives and the Parisi penalties. Transport minimality against every admissible competitor, including restriction or extension of that competitor. **Diffusion and moments.** Reindex the same process between nonnegative and real time, and stop it at one where required. Transport the integral equation on one full-measure event for all $t\in[0,1]$, path continuity, initial value, gradient and moment integrals. The diffusion comparison has a real version issue. The support predicate asks for a globally progressive process; the scalar predicate asks for adaptedness of the stopped process and almost-sure continuity on $[0,1]$. Restriction of a progressive support process is a plausible route in one direction. A converse must supply the required progressive version and its extension, then prove that the relevant integrals and moments are unchanged. It is not the literal identity of the two predicates. Likewise, equality of values for all $x$ is needed before transporting their derivatives; agreement at $(0,0)$ is insufficient. Once those obligations are proved, an application must use the same transported minimizer and associated diffusion in all premises. No such cross-model transport theorem is supplied here. The manuscript proof in §§3–7 and the scalar implementation's independent argument remain available without it. These distinctions come from the defining [support model][support-model] and [scalar model][value-model], rather than from their endpoint names.

The full-support theorem and scalar-value theorem use related but
different formal representations. Their mathematical conclusions can be
discussed together, but a direct formal implication would require the
coefficient, Brownian law, control value and diffusion translations
described in §12, with common witnesses. The finite Gaussian result
also needs its rooted energy identification before it says anything
about a QAOA circuit. The boundedness, regularization, synthesis and
transfer estimates in §8 are additional steps, with temperature-specific
hypotheses where the positive-temperature route is used.

Infinite support allows gaps. An indefinite curvature identity does not imply
strict convexity before expectation is controlled. An algebraic certificate
does not establish its analytic hypotheses. Coordinatewise convergence does
not control a growing coefficient sum. A finite-dimensional Gaussian law
does not identify an energy observable without its operator argument.
Separate witnesses cannot be merged silently. The order
$\forall\varepsilon\ \exists\text{finite word}\ \lim_{n\to\infty}$
cannot be replaced by a fixed-instance depth limit.

The local comparison in §11.1 concerns two printed finite-step displays;
it neither replaces the cited theorem's hypotheses nor supplies the
remaining circuit estimates.
